language model in Active Retrieval Augmented Generation

Zhengbao Jiang · 2023

A language model is a foundational component in natural language processing systems with remarkable abilities to comprehend and generate language, including long-form question answering, open-domain summarization, and chain-of-thought reasoning. Its central limitation is hallucination: despite memorized world knowledge, it can produce factually inaccurate output. In retrieval augmented generation, it pairs with a retriever, conditions on user input and retrieved documents, and generates answers; when more information is needed, it can generate retrieval queries and may use token probabilities, with low probability often indicating lack of knowledge, to trigger retrieval. In FLARE methods, it also generates temporary next sentences without retrieved documents and can use prior tokens as queries, though these may not match future intent. Forward-looking retrieval, hints, and future-oriented queries help it stay on topic, while generic instructions and exemplars are challenging.

Narrative, section by section

6 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Large language models have a remarkable ability to comprehend and generate language, but they tend to hallucinate and produce factually inaccurate output.

Introduction

Generative language models have become foundational components in natural language processing systems and have demonstrated abilities in long-form question answering, open-domain summarization, and chain-of-thought reasoning. Although they memorize some world knowledge during training, they still tend to hallucinate.

2 .. 2.3

The language model conditions on the user input and retrieved documents to generate the answer. In active retrieval augmented generation, it continually generates tokens using the current retrieved documents, the user input, and previous generation.

3 .. 3.3

The language model generates answers, retrieval queries, and temporary next sentences in the FLARE methods. Its token probabilities are used to estimate confidence, and low confidence can trigger retrieval.

4

The language model may use previously generated tokens as retrieval queries, although such queries might not reflect what it intends to generate in the future.

6 .. 6.2

Language models benefit from forward-looking retrieval because it helps them access information relevant to upcoming generation. The unit also finds that generic retrieval instructions and exemplars are challenging for language models, while hints and future-oriented queries help them stay on topic.

large language model in Enhancing Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models with Iterative Retrieval-Generation Synergy

Zhihong Shao, Yeyun Gong, Yelong Shen, Minlie Huang, Nan Duan, Weizhu Chen · 2023

A large language model is a generative language model that powers applications and produces reasoning, answers, search-related content, and phrases. Its central limitations are outdated or under-represented knowledge, substantial compute and data needs for continual updating, and hallucinations: plausible but non-factual text, especially in open-domain settings. It can be grounded in external knowledge through tools, retrieved information, and generation that guides retrieval. Its outputs may bridge semantic gaps between complex questions and supporting knowledge, though incorrect initial reasoning can mislead later retrieval. In an iterative process, it generates phrases in the first iteration to retrieve relevant knowledge, then successfully corrects outputs in the second. The experiments used a fixed black-box model not equally optimized for prompting; prompting-specific optimization is proposed to improve use of parametric and non-parametric knowledge.

Narrative, section by section

6 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Large language models are described as having limitations including outdated knowledge and hallucinations. They can be actively involved in retrieval by using generation to guide the retrieval of relevant knowledge.

1

Generative Large Language Models power numerous applications but lack knowledge that is under-represented in their training data and are prone to hallucinations, especially in open-domain settings. The unit studies methods for grounding their outputs in external knowledge.

2

LLMs power applications such as ChatGPT, Bing Chat, and CoPilot, but they require substantial compute and data for continual updating and tend to hallucinate plausible but non-factual text. They can be augmented with tools such as code interpreters and search engines, or with retrieved information, to offload subtasks and improve their input context.

4 / 4.1 .. 4.7

The large language model generates reasoning, answers, search-related content, and outputs used to adapt retrieval. Its generated outputs can bridge semantic gaps between complex questions and supporting knowledge, but incorrect initial reasoning can also mislead later retrieval.

5

The large language model, referred to as the LLM, generates phrases that help retrieve relevant knowledge in the second iteration and successfully corrects its outputs.

Limitations

The experiments used a fixed black-box large language model that may not have been equally optimized for different forms of prompting. The work proposes investigating prompting-specific gradient-based optimization to push performance further and enable more effective use of parametric and non-parametric knowledge.

large language models in Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding

Wenyu Huang, Mirella Lapata, Pavlos Vougiouklis, Nikos Papasarantopoulos, Jeff Z. Pan · 2023

Large language models, including GPT-4, can produce plausible but factually incorrect statements when lacking external knowledge. Hallucination is the central concern. Retrieval-augmented generation, using passages or knowledge graph triples, is presented to support reasoning, improve factuality, and train retrievers to reduce hallucinations.

Narrative, section by section

3 sections; each heading opens the text

Introduction

Large Language Models such as GPT-4 can still produce plausible-looking statements that are factually incorrect when they lack external knowledge.

Related Works

Large language models are discussed as a setting in which retrieval augmented generation can help address hallucination. Retrieved passages or knowledge graph triples can support their reasoning and increase prediction factuality.

Conclusion

Large language models are identified as an area where retrieval augmented methods are crucial. The proposed methods could be used to train retrievers that reduce hallucinations from large language models.

Large Language Models in Semantic Embeddings for Arabic Retrieval Augmented Generation

Hazem Abdelazim · 2023

Large Language Models are an evolving technology with impressive capabilities that have increased attention to Retrieval Augmented Generation. Through RAG, they access external knowledge sources, use retrieved information to generate contextually relevant responses, and are applied to downstream tasks. Their context-window limitations motivate continued RAG research. The process begins with information retrieval and then selects a model to comprehend retrieved context and answer a research query. Models include LLaMA, Falcon, GPT neoX, Bloom, vicuna, and FlanT5; Arabic support varies, and some APIs are paid. When retrieval misses relevant corpus portions, they may fail to find proper answers or confidently hallucinate wrong ones.

large language model in Retrieval Augmented Generation and Representative Vector Summarization for Large Unstructured Textual Data in Medical Education

S. S. Manathunga · 2023-08-01

Large language models are models that support zero-shot learning, content generation, chatbots, and general question answering. They retain learned knowledge in their weights as a parameterized knowledgebase, making later updates difficult and allowing plausible but factually inaccurate hallucinations. They generate answers from compiled prompts containing an original query and retrieved or summarized text; one without a non-parametric knowledge-base was compared with a retrieval-augmented generation model on clinical medicine and pharmacology queries.

Large language models are described as capable of zero-shot learning, content generation, and general question answering. They retain learned knowledge in model weights, can be difficult to update after training, and may produce factually inaccurate but plausible answers.

large language models in SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection

Akari Asai, Zeqiu Wu, Yizhong Wang, Avirup Sil, Hannaneh Hajishirzi · 2023-10-17

Large language models are language models that generate responses from solely encapsulated parametric knowledge, often producing factual inaccuracies despite larger models and datasets. They are evaluated across six tasks with multiple metrics, including supervised fine-tuned, instruction-tuned, proprietary, and retrieval-augmented systems. SELF-RAG enhances them through retrieval and self-reflection while retaining creativity and versatility, improving several tasks; smaller SELF-RAG models may attain greater factual precision through shorter, more grounded outputs.

Narrative, section by section

4 sections; each heading opens the text

ABSTRACT

Large language models often produce factually inaccurate responses because they rely solely on the parametric knowledge they encapsulate.

INTRODUCTION

State-of-the-art LLMs continue to struggle with factual errors despite increases in model and data scale.

SELF-RAG: LEARNING TO RETRIEVE, GENERATE AND CRITIQUE / 3.1 / PROBLEM FORMALIZATION AND OVERVIEW .. 3.3 / SELF-RAG INFERENCE

A large language model is enhanced by SELF-RAG with retrieval and self-reflection without sacrificing its original creativity and versatility.

RESULTS AND ANALYSIS / 5.1 / MAIN RESULTS .. 5.2 / ANALYSIS

The evaluated large language models include supervised fine-tuned models, instruction-tuned models, proprietary models, and retrieval-augmented systems. SELF-RAG improves over larger or otherwise strong language models on several tasks, although smaller SELF-RAG models can sometimes achieve higher factual precision because they generate shorter, more grounded outputs.

large language models in SELF-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection

Akari Asai, Zeqiu Wu, Yizhong Wang, Avirup Sil, Hannaneh Hajishirzi · 2023-10-17

Large language models are trained end-to-end to generate task outputs and intermittent reflection tokens. In SELF-RAG, they learn to decide when retrieval is needed, evaluate passages and outputs, and produce controllable responses, aiming to improve factual accuracy without harming versatility. Their unfactual outputs can cause misinformation or dangerous advice; they were trained and evaluated with Stability AI computing.

Narrative, section by section

4 sections; each heading opens the text

INTRODUCTION

The large language model is trained in an end-to-end manner to generate task outputs together with intermittent reflection tokens. SELF-RAG is intended to improve its factual accuracy without hurting its versatility.

RELATED WORK

Language models can be fine-tuned or used with retrieved passages for knowledge-intensive tasks. In SELF-RAG, an arbitrary language model is trained to decide when retrieval is needed, evaluate retrieved passages and generated outputs, and produce controllable responses.

ETHICAL CONCERNS

Large language models are associated with outputs whose lack of factuality can contribute to misinformation and incorrect or dangerous advice.

ACKNOWLEDGMENTS

The language models in this work were trained and evaluated using computing provided by Stability AI.

LLM in BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation

David Rau, Hervé Déjean, Nadezhda Chirkova, Thibault Formal, Shuai Wang, Stéphane Clinchant, Vassilina Nikoulina · 2024

LLM is a language model, specifically a parametric generative language model, that stores vast information, common-sense knowledge, and other knowledge in its parameters or weights. It generates a response from context segments and user input, and its knowledge can be accessed through prompting and question answering after alignment. This embedded knowledge is static, hard to inspect or update, and may be inaccurate or outdated. The records describe LLMs being enhanced with external knowledge through Retrieval-Augmented Generation and evaluated with retrieved documents or in closed-book settings. Different LLMs, retrieval systems, model sizes, and ten datasets are compared using a shared general prompt.

Narrative, section by section

6 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Large Language Models are enhanced with external knowledge through Retrieval-Augmented Generation. The unit includes LLMs among the components benchmarked in question-answering experiments.

Introduction

Large Language Models can store vast amounts of information from pretraining data in their weights and can provide answers through prompting after alignment. Their embedded knowledge is static, difficult to inspect or update, and may contain inaccurately memorized or outdated information.

Related Work

The unit discusses the growing interest in LLMs and compares their role with retrieval quality, including the relative impact of LLM size. It also notes that RAG studies vary in the LLMs used in their experimental setups.

Task Definition

The parametric generative language model θ generates a response r based on the context segments c and user input x, both embedded in the instruction template i.

A

The LLMs are evaluated with context provided through different retrieval systems. Different LLMs are compared across 10 datasets.

E

The large language model is evaluated with retrieved documents or in a closed-book setting using a shared general prompt. The evaluated models include Llama2-70B, Llama2-7B, Llama3-8B, Mixtral-8x7B, SOLAR-10.7B, and TinyLlama-1.1B.

Large Language Models in Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine

Guangzhi Xiong, Qiao Jin, Zhiyong Lu, Aidong Zhang · 2024

Large Language Models are information-seeking systems used online for searching and chatbot interactions, with strong general and medical question-answering capabilities. They achieve state-of-the-art performance across medical QA tasks and outperform BERT-based models by large margins, serving as reasoning engines rather than knowledge databases in the cited medical setting. However, they can generate plausible but factually incorrect responses and may lack the latest knowledge. In MEDRAG, listed models receive retrieved snippets prepended to inputs and use chain-of-thought prompting; the study evaluates their predictions, while generated rationales remain to be evaluated.

Narrative, section by section

5 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Large language models have achieved state-of-the-art performance on a wide range of medical question answering tasks, but they still face challenges from hallucinations and outdated knowledge.

Introduction

Large Language Models have transformed online information seeking and show strong question-answering capabilities in general and medical domains. They can nevertheless produce plausible but factually incorrect responses and may lack recent knowledge, such as updated clinical guidelines.

Related Work / Retrieval-augmented Generation .. Biomedical Question Answering

Large language models have outperformed BERT-based models by large margins on medical question answering. Biomedical QA datasets are used to evaluate both general and domain-specific large language models.

The MEDRAG Toolkit

The LLMs component includes GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Mixtral, Llama-2, MEDITRON, and PMC-LLaMA. Retrieved snippets are concatenated and prepended to their inputs, and chain-of-thought prompting is used for all listed models.

Limitations

The LLM receives retrieved documents as context in the vanilla RAG architecture and uses the multiple-choice options as input for the final prediction. The study evaluates LLMs within MEDRAG but notes that the rationales generated by MEDRAG remain to be evaluated.

large language models in Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs

Zheng Wang, Zhongyang Li, Zeren Jiang, Dandan Tu, Wei Shi · 2024

Large language models power personalized agents that use smartphone memories to improve downstream applications. They provide semantic understanding and reasoning for personal AI assistants, receiving questions with selected user memories and generating answers. Rather than relying on global knowledge, frozen models use retrieval-augmented generation to respond to changes in the EMG. Their fixed parameters remain unchanged during training, while answer quality evaluates and rewards memory selection.

large language models in DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models

Weihang Su, Yichen Tang, Qingyao Ai, Zhijing Wu, Yiqun Liu · 2024

Large language models are models used widely in AI applications that have advanced natural language processing and are effective across many tasks. They generate tokens using self-attention and built-in knowledge, producing coherent, plausible text but often factual errors and sometimes falling short on knowledge-intensive tasks. Retrieval augmentation addresses these limits by supplying external-corpus information. In dynamic retrieval augmented generation, retrieval determines whether and what to retrieve; the model records token probabilities and attention scores, receives external knowledge with a truncated answer, and continues generating.

Narrative, section by section

4 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Large Language Models generate text while the dynamic retrieval augmented generation paradigm determines whether and what information to retrieve for them.

Introduction

Large language models have advanced across many natural language processing tasks and have become important in numerous AI applications. They can generate coherent and plausible text that is factually incorrect, and DRAGIN is designed to augment them dynamically without further training, fine-tuning, or prompt engineering.

2 / 2.1 .. 2.2

Large language models are effective across many tasks but can fall short on knowledge-intensive tasks. Retrieval augmentation is used to provide them with information from external corpora.

3 .. 3.3

The large language model generates tokens while recording token probabilities and last-layer attention scores. After retrieval, it receives a prompt containing external knowledge and the truncated answer, then continues generating.

A language model is a pre-trained model that undergoes task-agnostic pretraining. It is used to generate distractor candidates through Generating and Ranking or Text2Text from a question stem and answer. In Retrieval Augmented Pretraining, it generates ground-truth distractors from masked retrieved text and an answer option, then supports triplet retrieval and supervised re-ranking.

A language model is pretrained in Retrieval Augmented Pretraining to generate ground-truth distractors from a masked retrieved sentence or passage, together with the answer option. A language model trained for distractor generation also generates candidate distractors for knowledge triplet retrieval, and it can be used for supervised triplet re-ranking.

large language models in Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation

Zhenrui Yue, Huimin Zeng, Yimeng Lu, Lanyu Shang, Yang Zhang, and Dong Wang · 2024

Large language models are language models that embed world knowledge in parameters through extensive pretraining and have achieved substantial improvements in language understanding and generation. They enhance performance across various scenarios, but struggle with fine-grained knowledge and frequently hallucinate because of limited knowledge and reasoning capabilities. In RARG, retrieval-augmented generation incorporates external knowledge and retrieved evidence, while reinforcement learning from human feedback aligns them to produce polite, factual, evidence-based responses.

Large language models are aligned to generate evidence-based responses in RARG. They generate responses using retrieved evidence.

Large language models are used in the evidence-based response generation module. They are aligned through reinforcement learning from human feedback to generate polite and factual responses using retrieved evidence.

Retrieval Augmented Generation

Large language models have achieved substantial improvements in language understanding and generation and can embed world knowledge in their parameters through extensive pretraining. They nevertheless struggle to capture fine-grained knowledge and frequently produce hallucinations.

Methodology / Preliminary .. Response Generation

They are described as frequently exhibiting hallucination behavior because of limitations in knowledge and reasoning capabilities. Retrieval-augmented text generation is used to incorporate external knowledge and improve the factuality of their outputs.

large language models in Generate-then-Ground in Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multi-hop Question Answering

Zhengliang Shi, Shuo Zhang, Weiwei Sun, Shen Gao, Pengjie Ren, Zhumin Chen, Zhaochun Ren · 2024

Large language models are models used to answer knowledge-intensive Multi-Hop Question Answering tasks. They matter because they contribute parametric knowledge, world knowledge, and deductive ability: they decompose complex questions, formulate fine-grained sub-questions, perform step-by-step reasoning, and generate immediate answers. However, they can generate non-factual statements, be misled by noisy or irrelevant retrieved evidence, struggle when document lists are lengthy, and face conflicts between internal knowledge and external documents. In GenGround, they begin from the current context and input question, generate simpler single-hop sub-questions and direct answers, then ground those predictions in retrieved documents. They use external documents and their parameters as complementary knowledge sources, revising answers when supporting established evidence is found. The process alternates answer generation or deduction with grounding and revision over several iterations until a final answer is derived. In sampled questions, they directly answer 28.7% correctly, correctly revise 24.5% of initially non-factual answers, and have a 5.6% error rate after revision.

Narrative, section by section

8 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Large language models face challenges on Multi-Hop Question Answering because of the extensive knowledge required. GenGround uses their parametric knowledge and enables them to alternate between generating answers and grounding them in retrieved documents.

Introduction

Large language models are used to decompose complex questions, formulate sub-questions, generate immediate answers, and revise those answers using evidence. The unit proposes using their world knowledge and deduction capability in a generate-then-ground framework.

2 / 2.1 .. 2.2

Large language models are used to decompose multi-hop questions, perform step-by-step reasoning, and generate answers from retrieved documents. They can generate non-factual statements, be misled by noisy evidence, and experience knowledge conflicts when combining internal knowledge with external documents.

3 .. 3.3

LLMs generate fine-grained sub-questions and answers during answer deduction, using world knowledge stored in their parameters. They also ground generated answers in retrieved documents and revise them when supporting evidence is found.

6 / 6.1 .. 6.3

Large language models are used for answer deduction, knowledge grounding, and answer generation in the evaluated framework. The text attributes part of the framework's effectiveness to their deductive abilities and parametric knowledge.

7 / 7.1 .. 7.3

Large language models combine knowledge stored in their parameters with information from external documents to answer questions. They directly answer 28.7% of sampled questions correctly, revise initially non-factual answers correctly for 24.5%, and have a 5.6% error rate after revision.

8

Large language models use their parametric knowledge together with external documents in GenGround. They alternate between formulating simpler single-hop questions, generating answers, and grounding those predictions in retrieved documents.

Ethics Statement

Language Learning Models use the framework to alternate between deducing answers and utilizing established evidence to revise those answers across several iterations.

LLM in PlanRAG: A Plan-then-Retrieval Augmented Generation for Generative Large Language Models as Decision Makers

Myeonghwa Lee, Seonho An, Min-Soo Kim · 2024

LLM is a model studied as a solution for decision making requiring complex data analysis and as a possible replacement for the human role in planning, data retrieval, and decision answering. It retrieves data from structured databases through data-analysis queries, but most RAG systems operate in a single-turn, non-iterative manner and were insufficient for this task. In PlanRAG, the language model performs planning and retrieval-based reasoning, generates plans, queries, answers, and re-planning decisions, and retrieves different nodes and edges by instance. Its use is limited by hallucination and potentially biased answers.

7 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

LLMs are studied as a solution for decision making that requires complex data analysis.

Introduction

A Large Language Model is proposed as a possible replacement for the human role in planning, data retrieval, and decision answering. The study investigates whether it can perform these decision-making steps end-to-end.

Methodology: PlanRAG

The language model in PlanRAG performs both planning and retrieval-based reasoning to reduce the side effects of using separate language models. It generates plans, data analysis queries, answers, and decisions about whether re-planning is needed.

Related Work

Language models are described as using RAG to retrieve external data and generate responses. The reviewed benchmarks did not consider language models querying over a large structured database, and the experiments found RAG insufficient for the decision-making task.

Conclusions

The paper explores the capability of large language models as a solution for decision making.

Limitations

The paper explores the capability of LLM as a solution for decision making.

Ethical Considerations

Language models have a hallucination issue and can potentially generate biased answers.

large language models (LLMs) in R2AG: Incorporating Retrieval Information into Retrieval Augmented Generation

Fuda Ye, Shuangyin Li, Yongqi Zhang, Lei Chen · 2024

Large language models are generally decoder-architecture generators that answer questions from inherent knowledge or supplied documents. In retrieval augmented generation, they receive the original query and retrieved documents, process all results, and generate answers using those documents. Although trained on vast corpora, they can hallucinate, struggle with updated knowledge in knowledge-sensitive tasks, and produce incorrect or potentially harmful answers. They also do not fully understand why retrievers provide particular documents; differences between retriever and model objectives and architectures can cause incomprehension. Processing all retrieved material exposes them to noise, information overload, and the lost-in-the-middle problem, especially with overly long documents. R2AG addresses this by integrating retrieval information into generation inputs, including when models remain frozen, and can align its R2-Former with the model through language modeling. Experiments use open- and closed-source models as RAG baselines and foundation models; stronger models and more effective retrievers improve R2AG performance. The method ultimately provides documents and retrieval information to enhance generation and support a comprehensive understanding of retrieved documents.

Narrative, section by section

7 sections; each heading opens the text

front matter .. Abstract

Large language models are augmented with external documents in retrieval augmented generation, but differences between their training objectives and architectures and those of retrievers can cause incomprehension during generation. R2AG integrates retrieval information into their generation process and is designed for scenarios where the models remain frozen.

Introduction

LLMs generate answers from inherent knowledge or supplied documents, but they do not fully understand why retrievers provide particular documents. In RAG, they must process and assess all retrieved results, making them vulnerable to noise, information overload, and the lost-in-the-middle problem.

Related Works / Retrieval Augmented Generation .. Enhanced RAG

Large language models can still produce hallucinations and struggle with updated knowledge in knowledge-sensitive tasks despite being trained on vast corpora. They use retrieved documents in Retrieval Augmented Generation to access flexible and up-to-date information.

R2AG / Problem Formulation and Overview .. Training Strategy

The LLM generates outputs from the query, documents, and retrieval information provided in its input embeddings. R2AG can align the R2-Former with the LLM through language modeling while either freezing the LLM or training both components together.

Experiments / Datasets and Metrics .. Discussions

The experiments use multiple open-source and closed-source LLMs as standard RAG baselines and foundation models. The results indicate that both stronger LLMs and more effective retrievers improve R2AG performance.

Conclusion and Future Work

LLMs receive retrieval information from retrievers through R2AG’s generation process. This integration helps R2AG capture a comprehensive understanding of retrieved documents.

Ethics Statement

LLMs can generate incorrect and potentially harmful answers. The proposed method provides them with retrieved documents and retrieval information to enhance their generation capability.

Kelong Mao, Zheng Liu, Hongjin Qian, Fengran Mo, Chenlong Deng, Zhicheng Dou · 2024

Large language models serve as generators in retrieval-augmented generation systems, where integrated retrieval can provide authoritative, up-to-date information. General models may lack updated domain-specific knowledge, deep understanding, and effective context use, and can be confused by irrelevant context. LLMs in RAGAS: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation

Shahul Es, Jithin James, Luis Espinosa-Anke, Steven Schockaert · 2024

LLMs are technology that receive knowledge from a reference corpus through RAG systems, using retrieved documents added to their input, including documents available only through APIs. This can keep LLM-based systems up to date and reduce hallucinations, because language models can struggle with events after training and rarely mentioned knowledge. They are studied for detecting hallucinations and estimating factuality or faithfulness, and can evaluate generated text and the quality aspects of RAGAS components. In evaluation, an LLM may extract statements, determine whether each can be inferred from context with a verification function, give an explanation and Yes/No verdict, generate potential questions, and extract relevant context sentences. LLMs can provide calibrated probabilities for multiple-choice questions, but judgments may depend on prompt design and answer order. Results can differ across runs because of API changes or neural-network randomness, so reproducibility, reliable software, structured JSON output, and careful review of limitations are critical; open models are ideally prioritized over paid APIs.

Narrative, section by section

7 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Large language models receive knowledge from a reference corpus through RAG systems. This access can help keep LLM-based systems up to date and reduce the risk of hallucinations.

opening

Language models can struggle to answer questions about events that occurred after training and to memorize knowledge that is rarely mentioned in the training corpus. Standard language models can use retrieved documents added to their input, including when they are available only through APIs.

2 / Estimating faithfulness using LLMs .. Automated evaluation of text generation systems

LLMs are studied for detecting hallucinations and estimating the factuality or faithfulness of generated responses. They are also used to evaluate qualities of generated text, although their judgments can be sensitive to prompt design and answer order.

3 .. Faithfulness

A large language model is prompted to evaluate the three quality aspects. In the implementation and experiments described, prompts were evaluated using the gpt-3.5-turbo-16k model available through the OpenAI API.

opening .. Context relevance

The LLM determines whether each statement can be inferred from the context and provides a brief explanation followed by a Yes/No verdict. It also generates potential questions from an answer and extracts context sentences relevant to a question.

5 .. 5.1

Large language models can produce different results across runs because of undocumented API changes or inherent neural-network randomness. Experiments therefore require attention to reliable software, reproducibility, and structured JSON output.

opening

LLMs are used to evaluate the different components of RAGAS and contribute to metrics that correlate highly with human judgements. Their known limitations make careful review of their suitability critical, with open models ideally prioritized over paid APIs.

LLM in RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Kiseung Kim and Jay-Yoon Lee · 2024

Large language models are models with 7B parameters or more and abundant parametric knowledge, including GPT and Llama. They are used in in-context learning and by RALM with concatenated context. A relevance estimator trained on a small language model can help them choose parametric knowledge when retrieved contexts have low confidence or are unreliable. Although FiD methods limit them because they require encoded data, their development renewed attention to RAG models that directly input context. Combined with a detachable relevance estimator, they improve performance.

Narrative, section by section

6 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

The relevance estimator (RE) can improve previously unreferenced large language models (LLMs). The decoding strategies can choose to rely on an LLM’s parametric knowledge rather than unrelated contexts.

Introduction

Large-language models are used by RALM with concatenated context in an in-context learning approach.

opening

Large language models can use a relevance estimator trained on a small language model. They can selectively rely on their parametric knowledge when retrieved contexts have low confidence.

5 / 5.1 .. 5.3

LLMs are described as having abundant parametric knowledge that can be directly used when retrieved contexts are unreliable. The largest model within each model family serves as the parametric knowledge base in the mixed strategy.

6

Large language models such as GPT and Llama face limitations with FiD methods that require encoded data. Their development has renewed attention to RAG models that can directly input context.

7

Modern large language models can be combined with the detachable RE module, which improves their performance.

Kurnia Muludi, Kaira Milani Fitria, Joko Triloka, Sutedi · 2024

Large Language Model is a language model technology that generates text from user commands and retrieved external information. In document question answering, it provides the generation mechanism in a Retrieval Augmented Generation approach combined with vector-store search, with ChatGPT used as the modified model. Modified document-processing methods require substantial resources and are challenging to implement widely. large language models in Retrieval-augmented generation in multilingual settings

Association for Computational Linguistics · 2024

Large language models are decoder-only Transformer models that generate responses from user queries and retrieved context. They are pretrained on unsupervised data, then tuned for instruction following and alignment with user preferences. In multilingual retrieval-augmented generation, they receive up-to-date or domain-specific knowledge, including five passages selected by a reranker, to improve factuality. Current state-of-the-art models are often English-centric or limited-language, though they may show multilingual capabilities from multilingual pretraining data; how many languages they support without reduced performance is unclear. They can be used off the shelf in zero-shot settings, tend toward verbose full-sentence answers, and were quantized to int4 in all experiments.

Narrative, section by section

6 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Large language models are the systems into which retrieval-augmented generation incorporates up-to-date or domain-specific knowledge. The work studies how multilingual retrieval-augmented generation can improve their factuality.

Introduction

Large language models can receive up-to-date or domain-specific knowledge through retrieval-augmented generation.

Related Work

Generator LLMs are identified as individual RAG pipeline components that are rather well developed for multilingual settings.

Multilingual RAG pipeline

The generator LLM generates the response from the user query and retrieved context. The studied models use decoder-only Transformer architectures pretrained on unsupervised data and tuned for instruction following and alignment with user preferences.

opening

Large language models may support multilingual capabilities even when they are pretrained and fine-tuned mostly on English data, because multilingual data may appear in pretraining. The text notes that the number of languages such models can support without reduced performance remains unclear.

4

The LLM receives the five passages selected by the reranker in its context during generation.

large language models in RetrievalQA: Assessing Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Short-form Open-Domain Question Answering

Zihan Zhang, Meng Fang, Ling Chen · 2024

Large language models are technology with distinct sizes and levels of pre-trained knowledge. Through large-scale pre-training, they encode extensive knowledge and can answer straightforward queries without retrieval, but they are static after training, can become outdated, and are weak on long-tail questions. When needed knowledge is absent, they should recognize the gap, say “I don’t know,” and request external retrieval. In retrieval-augmented generation, they answer using instructions, questions, and retrieved relevant documents, or skip retrieval when it is unnecessary. The records study their ability to judge this need: they perceive some knowledge boundaries, especially for new-world knowledge, but Vanilla prompting makes retrieval decisions unreliable. RetrievalQA is designed around missing knowledge, while TA-ARE helps assess retrieval necessity without calibration or additional training; noisy retrieved context can still interfere.

Narrative, section by section

7 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Large language models do not contain the knowledge needed to answer the questions in RetrievalQA, so external information must be retrieved. TA-ARE helps them assess whether retrieval is necessary without calibration or additional training.

Introduction

Large language models are augmented with retrieved relevant information in retrieval-augmented generation.

opening

Large language models encode extensive knowledge in their parameters through large-scale pre-training and can answer straightforward queries without retrieval. The unit studies whether they can reliably recognize when external retrieval is necessary.

Dataset Construction

LLMs are static after training and can quickly become outdated as the world changes. The dataset is designed so that the knowledge needed for many questions is absent from LLMs, requiring them to consult external resources.

RetrievalQA Challenges Adaptive RAG / 3.1 .. 3.4

An LLM generates answers from instructions, retrieved documents, and questions, or from instructions and questions when retrieval is skipped. The unit finds that LLMs can perceive some knowledge boundaries but are unreliable at making retrieval decisions through Vanilla prompting.

Limitations

LLMs may be able to answer some dataset questions without additional information. They may also be interfered with by noisy retrieved context.

Ethical Statement

LLMs are evaluated by the RetrievalQA dataset on their self-awareness ability to decide when to retrieve external resources.

Bolei He, Nuo Chen, Xinran He, Lingyong Yan, Zhenkai Wei, Jinchang Luo, and Zhen-Hua Ling · 2024

Large Language Models are a technology for natural language understanding, generation, and question answering. They have achieved major advances but usually suffer hallucinations, producing factually incorrect or externally inconsistent answers because of inappropriate training knowledge, overfitting, limited knowledge-generation abilities, and knowledge boundaries. Retrieval Augmented Generation incorporates external knowledge to enhance them.

Narrative, section by section

3 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Large Language Models are enhanced by Retrieval Augmented Generation through the incorporation of knowledge from external sources. Their knowledge boundary can contribute to answers that are inconsistent with external references.

Introduction

Large Language Models have achieved major advances in natural language understanding and generation, particularly in question answering. They can still generate factually incorrect answers because of persistent inappropriate knowledge and limited knowledge-generation abilities.

5 / Related Work

Large language models usually suffer from hallucinations. Their hallucinations have been attributed either to overfitting to hallucinations in training data or to reaching their knowledge boundaries.

large language models in Searching for Best Practices in Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Xiaohua Wang, Zhenghua Wang, Xuan Gao, Feiran Zhang, Yixin Wu, Zhibo Xu, Tianyuan Shi, Zhengyuan Wang, Shizheng Li, Qi Qian, Ruicheng Yin, Changze Lv, Xiaoqing Zheng, Xuanjing Huang · 2024

Large language models are systems that produce content and handle sufficiently specified translation requests from inherent capabilities. Their accuracy matters, but they are prone to outdated information and fabricated facts; increasing size alone does not fundamentally address hallucinations. They can be aligned with human preferences through reinforcement learning or lightweight alternatives. Retrieval-augmented generation enhances them through query-dependent retrievals: some queries can be answered without retrieval, while requests needing current or additional information require it. Long prompts can slow inference and reduce accuracy. Overall, RAG seeks to make their generated content more high-quality and reliable.

Narrative, section by section

7 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Large language models can be enhanced through query-dependent retrievals in RAG workflows.

Introduction

Generative large language models are described as prone to producing outdated information or fabricating facts, despite alignment with human preferences through reinforcement learning or lightweight alternatives.

Related Work

Large Language Models such as ChatGPT and LLaMA generate responses whose accuracy is important. Simply increasing their size does not fundamentally address hallucinations.

Retriever and Generator Fine-tuning

Large language models are discussed in relation to the application of RAG methods and the integration of RAG with LLMs.

RAG Workflow / Query Classification

Large language models can answer some queries without retrieval because of their inherent capabilities. For example, an LLM trained up to 2023 can translate “Sora was developed by OpenAI” without retrieval, while an introduction request about the same topic would require retrieval.

Summarization

Long prompts can slow the inference process of large language models and may prevent them from generating accurate responses.

Conclusion

Large language models are the systems whose generated content retrieval-augmented generation aims to make more high-quality and reliable.

Large language models (LLMs) have powerful in-context learning capabilities but are prone to hallucinate. Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are often used as the reader in retrieval-augmented generation systems because of their in-context learning capabilities. In TRACE, an LLM is prompted as a knowledge graph generator and as an autoregressive reasoning chain constructor.

references

Large language models are studied for retrieval-augmented generation, logical reasoning, information extraction, in-context retrieval, and reasoning over graphs. The unit also includes work showing that large language models can be distracted by irrelevant context and can learn temporal reasoning.

large language models in The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

Shenglai Zeng, Jiankun Zhang, Pengfei He, Yue Xing, Yiding Liu, Han Xu, Jie Ren, Shuaiqiang Wang, Dawei Yin, Yi Chang, Jiliang Tang · 2024

Large language models are language models with documented privacy risks. They can memorize pre-training corpora and private information in pre-training and fine-tuning data, then inadvertently reveal, recall, reproduce, or leak it through generation and data-extraction attacks. In retrieval-augmented generation, a model receives a user query together with retrieved context or data and combines that information with pre-trained knowledge to generate an answer. This augmentation can make outputs more accurate and relevant, but model behavior can expose retrieval records. The work examines leakage of training data and finds that retrieval augmentation can also reduce the output of memorized training-data information.

Narrative, section by section

4 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Large language models have known privacy risks, and retrieval-augmented generation can reshape their inherent generation behaviors. The work further finds that retrieval-augmented generation can mitigate leakage of their training data.

1 / Introduction

A large language model receives the original query together with retrieved data and uses its pre-trained knowledge and the retrieved information to generate a response. The unit reports that LLM behavior in RAG can expose retrieval records, while retrieval augmentation can reduce the output of memorized training data.

2 / Related Work / 2.1 / Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) .. 2.2 / Privacy Risk of Large Language Models

Large language models can produce more accurate and relevant outputs when enhanced with retrieval-augmented generation. They are also prone to memorizing and inadvertently revealing information from their pre-training corpora.

3 / Method / 3.1 / Background and Threat Model .. 3.3 / Privacy Leakage on LLM Training Data

The large language model M receives the retrieved context and user query concatenated together, represented as M(R(q, D) || q), and generates the answer. It is also examined for leakage of information from its training data.

Large language models are examined for privacy risks from reproducing memorized training data. large language models in Unified Active Retrieval for Retrieval Augmented Generation

Qinyuan Cheng · 2024

Large language models are language models, commonly based on decoder-only architecture, that have developed rapidly in coding, writing, and reasoning but can generate fabricated or non-factual information. They can be trained to assess whether they know answers and express this capability. UAR uses that assessment to decide when external retrieval is needed, while keeping model parameters fixed during classifier training.

Narrative, section by section

3 sections; each heading opens the text

Introduction

Large language models have developed rapidly and demonstrate abilities in coding, writing, and reasoning, but they often generate fabricated or non-factual information. The unit presents UAR as a framework that determines when they should use external retrieval rather than relying only on internal knowledge.

2 / 2.1 .. 2.3

Large language models can be trained to assess and express whether they know the answer to a question. The unit describes supervised fine-tuning, preference optimization, value heads, and other approaches used to improve this capability.

3 .. 3.3

The large language model has its parameters fixed during UAR classifier training. For decoder-only models, UAR avoids recomputing the original instruction after retrieved information is appended.

Large Language Models in Unsupervised Information Refinement Training of Large Language Models for Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Association for Computational Linguistics · 2024

Large Language Models are current mainstream decoder-only models used in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to provide additional knowledge and mitigate hallucination. They are pre-trained before RAG use, but that training does not clearly teach them to use retrieved texts of varied quality as references. Consequently, they can ignore or be misled by incorrect or noisy information, struggle to extract correct answers from long, complex texts, and fail to integrate their parameter knowledge when retrieved texts cannot address a task. The work proposes continuing unsupervised training so they become Information Refiners. In this role, they refine information through next-token prediction, learn from prefixes and retrieved texts, and use layer-wise word distributions to identify informative tokens. They are trained to extract relevant knowledge, remove irrelevant material, verify and rectify incorrect retrieved knowledge, complete missing knowledge, and use semantically relevant context to stimulate knowledge within their parameters. Across the scenarios, they verify, correct, and complete retrieved knowledge, then combine retrieved texts with knowledge in their parameters to solve questions. The intended result is an LLM that integrates both knowledge sources and generates text that is more concise, accurate, and complete regardless of retrieved texts' correctness, completeness, or usefulness.

Narrative, section by section

8 sections; each heading opens the text

Unsupervised Information Refinement Training of Large Language Models for Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Large Language Models are the subject of the work's unsupervised information refinement training.

Abstract

Large language models can ignore or be misled by retrieved information because their training does not clearly teach them how to use retrieved texts of varied quality. The unit proposes training them to act as Information Refiners that combine retrieved knowledge with model parameters.

Introduction

Large language models are used in RAG to provide additional knowledge and help mitigate hallucination, but their pre-training does not explicitly teach them to use retrieved texts as references. The unit proposes continuing their training so they can extract relevant information, correct errors, complete missing knowledge, and integrate retrieved information with knowledge in their parameters while preserving generalizability.

Related Work / Retrieval Augmented Generation .. Our INFO-RAG

Large language models are described as the current mainstream models based on a decoder-only architecture. INFO-RAG is designed to train them for information refinement in RAG.

Positive Information Gain in RAG

LLMs are expected to extract relevant knowledge, remove irrelevant information, verify retrieved knowledge, correct errors, complete omissions, and use semantically relevant context to stimulate knowledge within their parameters.

Unsupervised Learning .. Training Strategy

Large language models are trained to refine information and predict target sentence continuations from prefixes and retrieved texts. They are also used to calculate layer-wise word distributions for identifying informative tokens.

Conclusion

LLMs are viewed as “Information Refiner” systems that integrate knowledge from their model parameters and retrieved texts. They can generate texts that are more concise, accurate, and complete, regardless of the correctness, completeness, or usefulness of the retrieved texts.

Limitations

Large language models are the systems this paper aims to enable to perform information refinement in Retrieval-Augmented Generation through unsupervised training.

Davide Caffagni · 2024

Large Language Models are a model family and language models with remarkable language understanding and reasoning. They show impressive zero-shot textual performance, follow user-described tasks, and can be fine-tuned on varied natural-language tasks to assimilate instructions and generalize across domains. Instruction tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback support alignment. They underpin multimodal systems: multimodal LLMs extend them beyond text, using visual tokens and optionally retrieved passages or external-memory tokens as context while generating text autoregressively.

Abstract

LLMs are extended by multimodal LLMs to work beyond the pure textual modality. In Wiki-LLaVA, retrieved passages are used as additional context for the LLM.

Large Language Models have demonstrated impressive performance on zero-shot textual tasks. They can be fine-tuned on varied tasks described through natural language, enabling them to assimilate instructions and generalize across multiple domains.

2. Related Work

Large language models such as ChatGPT, GPT-4, Flan-T5, Vicuna, LLaMA, and Alpaca have advanced language understanding and reasoning through techniques including instruction tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback. They have also been used as the foundation for multimodal systems.

3. Proposed Method .. 3.2. Training

The large language model generates text autoregressively based on visual tokens, the system and user prompt, and optionally retrieved external-memory tokens. LLaVA uses Vicuna as its pre-trained large language model.

Large Language Models in Merging Mixture of Experts and Retrieval Augmented Generation for Enhanced Information Retrieval and Reasoning

Xingyu Xiong and Mingliang Zheng · 2024-02-23

Large Language Models are deep learning architectures and models with vast parameter counts that demonstrate natural language processing, generation, comprehension, translation, and summarization. They can generate coherent, fluent text, but their most important limitations concern retrieving and processing specific information from vast datasets, integrating and reasoning over it, and handling complex queries needing deep understanding and contextual awareness. They may lack accurate external-source retrieval without explicit training, produce plausible but factually incorrect information, struggle to maintain context and provide accurate references, rely on static training data, and have gaps in deep knowledge, technical expertise, logical deduction, and problem-solving. The study begins by establishing these capabilities and limitations, then examines Retrieval Augmented Generation integrated with a Mixture of Experts architecture as a way to address traditional model limitations. It presents hybrid architectures and possible integration with structured knowledge bases as pathways for improved training and design, concluding that MoE and RAG integration can support future research and applications involving more sophisticated, versatile models.

Narrative, section by section

6 sections; each heading opens the text

front matter

Large Language Models is listed as a keyword for the research article.

Merging Mixture of Experts and Retrieval Augmented Generation for Enhanced Information Retrieval and Reasoning / Abstrac

The study examines the integration of Retrieval Augmented Generation into a Large Language Model with a Mixture of Experts architecture. It presents the integration as a way to address limitations of traditional large language models.

I. INTRODUCTION

Large Language Models demonstrate strong capabilities in natural language processing, generation, comprehension, translation, and summarization. They continue to face challenges in retrieving and processing specific information from large datasets and in integrating and reasoning over that information.

II. RELATED WORK / A. Limitations of LLMs in Information Retrieval and Reason- .. C. RAG

Large language models generate coherent and fluent text but have limited ability to retrieve accurate information from external sources without explicit training. They may produce plausible but factually incorrect information, struggle with context, references, data recency, logical deduction, and complex problem-solving, and show diminishing retrieval improvements beyond a certain model size.

V. DISCUSSION / A. Enhancements in Model Performance .. B. Implications for AI Application Development

Large language models are described as having limitations in handling complex queries requiring deep understanding and contextual awareness. The unit presents hybrid architectures as a potential way to improve their training and design.

VI. CONCLUSION

Large language models are the broader class of systems whose capabilities the study seeks to enhance through the integration of MoE and RAG. The study presents its findings as a foundation for future research and applications involving more sophisticated and versatile models.

Large language models are described as having limitations in factual reliability and contextual appropriateness. The unit presents weighted RAG as a scalable way to improve these properties and increase their usefulness and trustworthiness in professional and high-stakes applications.

large language models in Retrieval augmented text-to-SQL generation for epidemiological question answering using electronic health records

Angelo Ziletti · 2024-06-21

Large language models are language models used to answer epidemiological questions through text-to-SQL generation and retrieval augmented generation. Leading models are evaluated with simple or advanced prompts, in-domain or out-of-domain demonstrations, retrieved examples, and up to three compiler-feedback self-corrections for non-executable SQL. They generate SQL with medical-entity placeholders and can produce answers from retrieved data after further prompting. Benchmarking finds retrieval augmented generation improves performance over static instruction prompting, while demonstrations also improve results. Despite these gains, they are not yet sufficiently accurate for unsupervised use.

Language models are used in the methodology for answering epidemiological questions through text-to-SQL generation and retrieval augmented generation. The findings indicate that they are not yet sufficiently accurate for unsupervised use, although retrieval augmented generation may improve their capabilities.

1

Large language models are evaluated through extensive benchmarking of the approach. The benchmarking confirms the performance improvement associated with retrieval augmented generation over static instruction prompting.

The unit evaluates GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4 Turbo, GeminiPro 1.0, Claude 2.1, Mixtral 8x7B, and Mixtral Medium. They receive simple or advanced prompts and may use retrieved examples and compiler feedback.

5

LLMs are used for prompting-based text-to-SQL methods, which often outperform specialized fine-tuned models. In-domain and out-of-domain demonstrations improve their performance, and Gao et al. (2023) examined retrieval scenarios for selecting in-domain demonstrations.

Large Language Models in FACTS About Building Retrieval Augmented Generation-based Chatbots

Rama Akkiraju, Anbang Xu, Deepak Bora, Tan Yu, Lu An, Vishal Seth, Aaditya Shukla, Pritam Gundecha, Hridhay Mehta, Ashwin Jha, Prithvi Raj, Abhinav Balasubramanian, Murali Maram, Guru Muthusamy, Shivakesh Reddy Annepally, Sidney Knowles, Min Du, Nick Burnett, Sean Javiya, Ashok Marannan, Mamta Kumari, Surbhi Jha, Ethan Dereszenski, Anupam Chakraborty, Subhash Ranjan, Amina Terfai, Anoop Surya, Tracey Mercer, Vinodh Kumar Thanigachalam, Tamar Bar, Sanjana Krishnan, Jasmine Jaksic, Nave Algarici, Jacob Liberman, Joey Conway, Sonu Nayyar and Justin Boitano · 2024-07-10

Large Language Models are technology and key components of enterprise chatbot systems. They understand user intents from simple natural-language prompts, synthesize enterprise content, and generate coherent, factual, and logical responses. In RAG pipelines, they generate answers from retrieved enterprise information, so quality depends on retrieval relevance and the final prompt. They may be fine-tuned and used in NVIDIA bots, with selectable models in NVInfo Bot and Scout Bot. Large and small models differ in accuracy and latency, while prompt-only guardrails are not followed consistently.

Narrative, section by section

5 sections; each heading opens the text

ABSTRACT

Large Language Models are key components in enterprise chatbot systems and may be fine-tuned for improved performance. The unit reports empirical results on accuracy-latency tradeoffs between large and small LLMs using enterprise data.

INTRODUCTION

Large language models understand user intents through simple natural-language prompts and can synthesize enterprise content coherently. Their generative capabilities help construct coherent, factual, and logical responses, while earlier language models lacked the accuracy, robustness, and reliability needed for broad enterprise use.

CASE STUDY

LLMs are used with RAGs in all three NVIDIA bots, and multiple LLM models can be selected in NVInfo Bot and Scout Bot.

ENSURING FRESHNESS OF ENTERPRISE .. 3.1

Large language models generate responses from retrieved enterprise information in a RAG pipeline. Their response quality depends heavily on the relevancy of the retrieved content and on the quality of the final prompt.

CONCLUSIONS

The paper empirically analyzes large and small LLMs, revealing trade-offs between accuracy and latency.

Soroosh Tayebi Arasteh · 2024-07-22

Large language models are a medical and radiological technology that encodes clinical knowledge and can extract structured information from radiological reports, improve data mining and diagnostic accuracy, detect speech-recognition errors, support differential diagnosis from imaging patterns, and serve as medical-information curators. Their central limitation is reliance on internal knowledge derived from static training datasets, which may be outdated, incomplete, inaccurate, or biased; inaccurate information and perpetuated bias are prominent risks in radiology. The records therefore emphasize using them as scientific reasoning engines with external sources rather than as knowledge databases. In radiological question answering, models including GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, Mistral-7B-instruct-v0.2, Mixtral-8x7B-instruct-v0.1, Llama3-8B, and Llama3-70B were evaluated with and without RadioRAG using RSNA-RadioQA and ExtendedQA. Assessment covered accuracy, source suitability, and willingness to state "I don't know" when evidence was insufficient. RadioRAG generally improved diagnostic performance, though gains varied by model and dataset, and irrelevant retrieved context could still produce incorrect responses.

Narrative, section by section

6 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Large language models are described as often generating outdated or inaccurate information from static training datasets. In this evaluation, they generally benefited from access to domain-specific information through RadioRAG, although the degree of improvement varied by model.

1. Introduction

Large language models have shown potential for extracting structured information from radiological reports, improving data mining and diagnostic accuracy, and enabling more reliable speech recognition. Their use is limited by risks of inaccurate information and bias, and their internal knowledge may be incomplete or biased. The unit proposes using them as reasoning engines with access to external sources.

2. Materials and Methods / 2.1. RSNA Cases .. 2.6. Code and Data Availability

Large language models were evaluated in conventional question-answering and RadioRAG settings using RSNA-RadioQA and ExtendedQA. Their responses were assessed for accuracy, source suitability, and their ability to state “I don't know” when information was insufficient.

3. Results / 3.1. Dataset Characteristics .. 3.5. Comparison to Human Performance

The large language models evaluated were GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, Mistral-7B-instruct-v0.2, Mixtral-8x7B-instruct-v0.1, Llama3-8B, and Llama3-70B. Their diagnostic performance generally improved with RadioRAG, although the magnitude and statistical significance of improvement varied by model and dataset.

4. Discussion

Large language models were evaluated with and without RadioRAG on radiological question-answering tasks. RadioRAG-powered models generally outperformed their conventional counterparts, but their responses could still be incorrect when retrieved context was irrelevant.

references

The references describe large language models in radiology, medicine, clinical research, medical question answering, scientific reasoning, and clinical decision-making. They also address their ethical considerations, risks, hallucinations, evaluation, retrieval augmentation, and use in autonomous clinical agents.

Large Language Models (LLM) in SDG target detection in environmental reports using Retrieval-augmented Generation with LLMs

Darío Garigliotti · 2024-08-16

Large Language Models (LLMs) are large language models and a dominant technology in natural language processing, increasingly important across areas and domains. They are a dominant component of approaches for multiple linguistic tasks, with state-of-the-art performance in text classification, textual entailment, and question answering. LLMs implicitly store vast information in billions of parameters trained on large general-purpose corpora. They power the text-generation component of Retrieval-augmented Generation: retrieved items are added to a prompt, and the model generates answers with correct identifiers. Their current capabilities are evaluated for SDG target evidence identification and SDG target detection, including identifying relevant passages or SDG targets and comparing generation-component choices.

Narrative, section by section

4 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Large Language Models (LLMs) are presented as a dominant component in approaches for multiple linguistic tasks. The paper evaluates their current capabilities for SDG target evidence identification and SDG target detection.

1

Large Language Models power the text-generation component of Retrieval-augmented Generation. They are described as the dominant technology in natural language processing and as showing state-of-the-art performance in multiple tasks.

2

LLMs store extensive information implicitly in billions of parameters trained on large general-purpose corpora, enabling strong performance on tasks such as text classification, textual entailment, and question answering. In the addressed tasks, an LLM uses retrieved items added to the prompt to generate answers containing correct identifiers.

3 / 3.1 .. 3.3

A Large Language Model generates answers identifying relevant passages or SDG targets in the two tasks. It is also the generation component whose choice is evaluated in the experiments.

Large Language Models in Medical Graph RAG: Towards Safe Medical Large Language Model via Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Junde Wu, Jiayuan Zhu, Yunli Qi, Jingkun Chen, Min Xu, Filippo Menolascina, Vicente Grau · 2024-10-15

Large Language Models are language models built on Transformer architectures that have accelerated natural language processing and enabled many AI applications. They matter in Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation, where they help organize data into graphs and support semantic chunking, entity and relationship extraction, tag summarization, and response generation. In medicine, specialized models including BioGPT, PMC-LLaMA, BioMedLM, and Med-PaLM 2 address a demanding domain, but finite context windows cannot hold vast knowledge bases and responses must be precise, non-creative, and verifiable. Many models are fine-tuned by large organizations, while recent work explores cost-efficient approaches without fine-tuning.

Narrative, section by section

4 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Large Language Models are used by Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation to organize Retrieval-Augmented Generation data into graphs. MedGraphRAG is intended to enhance their ability to generate evidence-based medical responses.

Introduction

Large language models have advanced natural language processing and enabled numerous AI applications, but they face significant challenges in specialized fields such as medicine. Their finite context windows cannot accommodate the vast knowledge bases of specialized domains, and their medical responses must remain precise, non-creative, and verifiable.

Method / Medical Graph Construction / Step1: Semantic Document Chunking .. Step6: U-Retrieval

Large language models impose context limitations that motivate chunking medical documents. The method also uses language models for semantic consistency decisions, entity extraction, relationship identification, tag summarization, and response generation.

Related Work / LLM for Medicine .. Retrieval-augmented generation

Large language models built on Transformer architectures have advanced rapidly and have led to specialized medical models such as BioGPT, PMC-LLaMA, BioMedLM, and Med-PaLM 2. Recent research has also explored cost-efficient approaches that do not require fine-tuning.

Generative Large Language Models in BlendFilter: Advancing Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models via Query Generation Blending and Knowledge Filtering

Haoyu Wang · 2024-11

Generative Large Language Models are language models and LLMs that show proficiency in summarization, dialogue systems, and question answering. Their finite pre-training corpora limit comprehensive, dynamic worldly knowledge. In retrieval-augmented approaches, they generate answers and augmented query contexts, interact with retrievers, decompose or rewrite questions, assess retrieval needs, and filter retrieved knowledge before producing final answers. Their self-evaluations may be unreliable, but their knowledge-filtering capabilities support BlendFilter by removing extraneous retrieved content without fine-tuning.

Narrative, section by section

4 sections; each heading opens the text

1

Generative Large Language Models have shown proficiency in summarization, dialogue systems, and question answering. Their finite pre-training corpora limit their ability to capture and maintain comprehensive worldly knowledge, particularly because that knowledge is dynamic.

2

Large Language Models are used to generate answers with retrieved knowledge and to interact actively with retrievers. They can decompose questions, rewrite or augment queries, assess retrieval needs, and filter knowledge, although their self-evaluations may be unreliable and their capabilities affect performance.

3 .. 3.4

The Large Language Model generates answers, produces externally and internally knowledge-augmented query contexts, filters retrieved knowledge, and generates final answers from filtered knowledge. It is used without fine-tuning and is treated as an effective knowledge filter.

5

Large language models provide the setting in which BlendFilter enhances retrieval-augmented generation. BlendFilter’s self-reliant knowledge filtering module exploits their inherent capabilities to refine retrieved knowledge by eliminating extraneous content.

large language models in RAG-HAT: A Hallucination-Aware Tuning Pipeline for LLM in Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Juntong Song, Xingguang Wang, Juno Zhu, Yuanhao Wu, Xuxin Cheng, Randy Zhong, and Cheng Niu · 2024-11

Large language models are transformer-based models that generate text. By scaling model size and training data, they have achieved significant milestones across tasks, yet hallucination remains a continuing challenge. Retrieval-augmented generation can integrate up-to-date information and organize local information coherently, but models may still distort or misinterpret sources and produce inaccurate outputs, posing risks in high-trust scenarios. Detection and mitigation use probabilities, consistency prompts, and training for more factual answers.

Narrative, section by section

3 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Large language models benefit from the up-to-date information integrated by retrieval-augmented generation. Even with RAG, they may distort or misinterpret source content and produce inaccurate outputs, creating risks in high-trust scenarios.

Introduction

Transformer-based Large Language Models have achieved significant milestones in various tasks by scaling up model size and training data. They continue to face challenges, particularly hallucination.

Related Work / Hallucination Detection .. Hallucination Mitigation

They are the subject of the reviewed detection and mitigation methods. Their probabilities may be used to detect hallucinations, they may be prompted to evaluate answer consistency, and they may be trained to detect or produce more factual answers.

large language models in Retrieval Augmented Generation or Long-Context LLMs?

Zhuowan Li · 2024-11-12/2024-11-16

Large language models are evaluated for long-context understanding and retrieval-augmented generation. They use retrieval to access external information cheaply, while large-scale pretraining may strengthen internal long-context capability. Relevant retrieved information supports language modeling and question answering. Recent models including Gemini-1.5 and GPT-4 show exceptional long-context understanding, but models learn different internal knowledge and therefore yield different numbers of non-commonsense questions.

Large Language Models in HyPA-RAG: A Hybrid Parameter Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation System for AI Legal and Policy Applications

Rishi Kalra, Zekun Wu, Ayesha Gulley, Airlie Hilliard, Xin Guan, Adriano Koshiyama, Philip Treleaven · 2024-11-16

Large Language Models are models capable of processing and generating human-like text, storing vast information in parameters through extensive pre-training. They excel at text generation and question-answering across multiple domains. They affect law and policy, where language complexity and large text volumes are prevalent, and are used for legal judgment prediction, document drafting, and contract analysis. They have been adapted through fine-tuning, retrieval augmentation, prompt engineering, and agentic methods. Their effectiveness in AI legal and policy applications is limited by rapid knowledge obsolescence, hallucinations, and inadequate reasoning in complex contexts. In the AI Legal and Policy Corpus, an LLM processes final selected chunks and knowledge graph triplets within its context window.

large language models in CausalRAG: Integrating Causal Graphs into Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Nengbo Wang, Xiaotian Han, Jagdip Singh, Jing Ma, Vipin Chaudhary · 2025

Large language models are language models that have rapidly advanced and revolutionized natural language processing, enabling many applications. They rely on pre-trained knowledge, which limits integration and reasoning over dynamically updated external information. In Retrieval-Augmented Generation, they can produce relevant-looking but superficial answers lacking essential details when retrieval is poor or retrieved content is inaccurately assessed. They benefit from external knowledge retrieval for knowledge-intensive tasks, though they may struggle to generalize from correlation to causation across datasets. In CausalRAG, a large language model parses text into nodes and edges, identifies and estimates causal paths, helps construct a refined causal graph, and generates a causal summary. As they evolve, they support larger inputs, but emerging domain-specific knowledge and additional inference calls can limit effectiveness and raise computational costs.

Narrative, section by section

6 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Large language models have revolutionized natural language processing. They are discussed as the underlying models whose capabilities can be enhanced through Retrieval-Augmented Generation.

Introduction

Large language models have advanced rapidly and revolutionized natural language processing, enabling a wide range of applications. Their reliance on pre-trained knowledge limits their ability to integrate and reason over dynamically updated external information.

opening

Large language models in RAG frameworks often generate seemingly relevant but shallow responses that lack essential details. The unit identifies poor retrieval and inaccurate assessment of retrieved content as primary reasons for this behavior.

Related Work / Retrieval-Augmented Generation .. Rethinking Graph-based RAGs

Large language models benefit from external knowledge retrieval in knowledge-intensive tasks. Existing work also uses them for causal discovery, causal effect estimation, iterative retrieval, retrieval supervision, and generation, but the unit notes limitations in their ability to generalize from correlation to causation across datasets.

Methodology .. Retrieving Context Causally

A large language model parses document text to identify nodes and infer edges. It also identifies and estimates causal paths, constructs a refined causal graph, and generates the causal summary.

Conclusion and Future Work

LLMs provide the internal knowledge used to construct graphs and identify causal relationships in CausalRAG. Their limitations with emerging domain-specific knowledge, such as in medicine or law, may constrain effectiveness, and additional LLM calls during inference increase computational costs.
