large language models in DioR: Adaptive Cognitive Detection and Contextual Retrieval Optimization for Dynamic Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Hanghui Guo, Jia Zhu, Shimin Di, Weijie Shi, Zhangze Chen, Jiajie Xu · 2025

Large language models are generative models that create text, dialogue, and summaries and perform strongly on downstream tasks. Their central limitation is that they are static: they lack real-time learning, cannot incorporate or integrate new or up-to-date information during generation, and may produce inaccurate, fabricated, or hallucinated content, especially when uncertain or unfamiliar. Their reasoning is a target for improved effectiveness and reliability. The records describe DioR, a Dynamic Retrieval-augmented Generation method that assesses model confidence before answering, monitors generation for likely hallucinations, and retrieves useful external knowledge when needed. Experiments compare question answering with and without DioR, using token probabilities to trigger retrieval. The work concludes that DioR helps reduce hallucinations and enhance reasoning, while step-by-step reasoning is intended to further improve reliability.

Narrative, section by section

7 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Large language models benefit from Dynamic Retrieval-augmented Generation (RAG) because it helps mitigate hallucinations during generation. DioR is designed to determine when retrieval is needed and what retrieval is useful for them.

Introduction

Large language models demonstrate capabilities in text creation, dialogue generation, and summarization, but they remain static and cannot learn in real time. They may lack up-to-date information and generate inaccurate or fabricated content in unfamiliar scenarios.

Related Work

Large language models show outstanding performance on downstream tasks, but they cannot integrate new information and are therefore prone to generating hallucinations.

Proposed Method: DioR / Adaptive cognitive detection / Is LLM confident in answering this? .. Post-retrieval

Large language models are assessed for confidence before answering and monitored during generation for likely hallucinations. Their generated content is supported with retrieved external knowledge when the detection process indicates that retrieval is needed.

Experiment / Experimental Setups .. Ablation Experiment

The large language model is evaluated on question-answering tasks with and without DioR and is used to generate tokens whose probabilities can trigger retrieval. The text presents DioR as helping address hallucinations while enhancing reasoning.

Conclusion and Future work

The paper examines methods for reducing hallucinations in LLMs. DioR is designed to determine when LLMs need retrieval and what information should be retrieved.

Limitations

The proposed step-by-step reasoning approach is intended to improve the overall effectiveness and reliability of large language models’ reasoning.

LLMs in Fact, Fetch, and Reason: A Unified Evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Satyapriya Krishna, Kalpesh Krishna, Anhad Mohananey, Steven Schwarcz, Adam Stambler, Shyam Upadhyay, Manaal Faruqui · 2025

LLMs are models, including large language models, trained on vast amounts of internet data. They have significantly improved cognitive and natural language processing tasks and are increasingly used to enhance retrieval-augmented generation, especially where factual accuracy and sophisticated reasoning matter. The records evaluate them on FRAMES questions requiring factuality, retrieval, and reasoning across multiple constraints. In synthetic dataset generation, they produced coherent questions from multiple articles, but many questions and answers were hallucinated; cleaned synthetic questions yielded approximately 32% accuracy. A reported baseline reached 0.408 accuracy without retrieval. Although multi-step retrieval and reasoning bring moderate improvements, state-of-the-art LLMs still struggle substantially with complex, multi-hop reasoning.

Narrative, section by section

5 sections; each heading opens the text

Large Language Models have shown significant improvements across cognitive tasks and are increasingly used to enhance retrieval-augmented generation capabilities. In the reported baseline, they achieve 0.408 accuracy without retrieval.

1

2

3 .. 3.2

5

State-of-the-art LLMs struggle significantly with the complex, multi-hop reasoning tasks in FRAMES. They achieve only moderate improvements when multi-step retrieval and reasoning strategies are used.

large language model in GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation

Zhili Shen · 2025

The large language model is a component of GEAR and SyncGE for retrieval-augmented question answering. It receives relevant passages, reads passages and queries, summarizes knowledge triples, locates initial triples and nodes, and guides graph expansion. During GEAR’s multi-step process, it produces proximal triples, determines answerability, supplies reasoning, rewrites queries, and links gist-memory triples with multi-hop passages. From initial retrieval through synchronized graph reasoning and termination, it supports gist-memory construction, improved retrieval, and fewer tokens than HippoRAG w/ IRCoT.

Narrative, section by section

5 sections; each heading opens the text

Introduction

Large Language Models benefit from Retrieval-augmented Generation in Question Answering tasks. Within GEAR, an LLM locates initial triples, while the framework uses a generic semantic model for subsequent graph expansion.

Related Work / Retrieval-augmented Models for QA / Multi-hop QA with LLMs and Graphs

Language models are used to generate pseudo-documents for query expansion, and their inputs can be augmented with relevant passages.

Retrieval with Synchronised Graph .. Reasoning for Termination / Query Re-writing / After Termination

The large language model reads retrieved passages and queries to produce proximal triples. It also determines answerability, supplies relevant reasoning, and rewrites queries during GEAR's multi-step process.

Discussion / What makes GEAR work? .. Is GEAR efficient?

LLMs are used by SyncGE to locate initial nodes. Within GEAR, the LLM reads multi-hop contexts and links proximal triples in gist memory with passages, and GEAR uses fewer LLM tokens than HippoRAG w/ IRCoT.

Conclusion

The large language model synchronizes passage information with triples through SyncGE and guides the exploration of initial nodes for graph expansion. Its use within GEAR also supports gist-memory construction and contributes to improved retrieval with fewer tokens.

large language model in GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Yuntong Hu, Zhihan Lei, Zheng Zhang, Bo Pan, Chen Ling, Liang Zhao · 2025

Large Language Models (LLMs) are language models that perform graph-based reasoning and can encode textual node and edge attributes, supporting classification, knowledge graph creation, graph reasoning, and zero-shot graph answering. They demonstrate graph reasoning especially with hierarchical text structures, but training on large text corpora does not inherently provide understanding of complex graph-structured data because text lacks explicit topological information. They also struggle with factual errors owing to training-data limitations and lack of real-time knowledge. GRAG addresses these limits by providing textual graphs through complementary text and graph views, including concatenated graph and text embeddings, to improve understanding of relationships and guide generation. Through these views, LLMs more effectively comprehend and utilize graph context; a frozen LLM enhanced by GRAG can outperform fine-tuned LLMs with reduced training cost.

Narrative, section by section

5 sections; each heading opens the text

front matter .. GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation / Abstract

Large Language Models receive textual graphs through complementary text and graph views in GRAG. These views enable them to more effectively comprehend and utilize graph context.

Introduction

Large Language Models demonstrate capabilities in various reasoning tasks, including graph-based data, but struggle with factual errors because of limitations in training data and lack of real-time knowledge. In this unit, they are provided with textual and graph prompts through GRAG to improve understanding of relationships in networked documents.

2 / 2.1 .. 2.3

LLMs encode textual node and edge attributes, benefiting classification and knowledge graph creation, while their contextual reasoning capabilities support graph reasoning and zero-shot graph answering. However, training on text does not inherently equip them to understand or reason about complex graph-structured data because textual data lacks explicit topological information.

4.2

It can reason over graphs, particularly when texts are organized in hierarchical structures such as trees. It receives concatenated graph and text embeddings to guide generation.

6

Large Language Models (LLMs) are enhanced by GRAG through access to graph and text views of a textual graph. A frozen LLM enhanced by GRAG can outperform fine-tuned LLMs at a reduced training cost.

large language models in HYBGRAG: Hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Textual and Relational Knowledge Bases

Meng-Chieh Lee, Qi Zhu, Costas Mavromatis, Zhen Han, Soji Adeshina, Vassilis N. Ioannidis, Huzefa Rangwala, Christos Faloutsos · 2025

Large language models are language models that can use Retrieval-Augmented Generation to access unstructured-document information, address unknown facts, and solve Open-Domain Question Answering. They can also be prompted to identify a hybrid question’s relational aspect, topic entities, and useful relations for knowledge-graph subgraph extraction, though refinement may be needed when textual and relational aspects are not distinguished. They support KBQA, planning, and self-reflection; as critics, pre-trained models may give suboptimal, overly implicit feedback without external tools, fine-tuning labels, and careful design. Related work covers retrieval, graph reasoning, self-correction, and iterative refinement.

Narrative, section by section

4 sections; each heading opens the text

1

Large language models can use Retrieval-Augmented Generation to access information from an unstructured document database. This allows them to address unknown facts and solve Open-Domain Question Answering with additional textual information.

2 / 2.1 .. 2.3

A large language model is prompted to identify the relational aspect of a hybrid question, including topic entities and useful relations for subgraph extraction. In the described experiment, it can require refinement because it may fail to distinguish textual and relational aspects.

5

Large language models are used to support KBQA, planning, and self-reflection. Pre-trained LLMs can serve as critics, but without external tools or labels for fine-tuning and without careful design, their self-evaluation can be suboptimal and their feedback overly implicit.

References

The unit cites research on large language model scaling, few-shot learning, chain-of-thought reasoning, long-context behavior, distraction by irrelevant context, and tool-assisted agents. It also references methods that use large language models for retrieval, graph reasoning, self-correction, and iterative refinement.

large language models in Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models

Zahra Khalila, Arbi Haza Nasution, Winda Monika, Aytug Onan, Yohei Murakami, Yasir Bin Ismail Radi, Noor Mohammad Osmani · 2025

Large language models are general-purpose models that handle activities including summarization, translation, domain-specific question answering, annotation, and response generation from retrieved descriptions. In the study, 13 open-source models are used for Quranic-studies queries in a Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework, operating zero-shot without fine-tuning on the dataset. Because Quranic studies are sensitive and domain-specific, the central concerns are accuracy, contextual relevance, authenticity, distortion, and hallucination. The models are assessed through human evaluation of Context Relevance, Answer Faithfulness, and Answer Relevance, and grouped by parameter size as small, medium, or large. Performance varies by size: larger models generally provide higher-quality, more accurate and contextually faithful responses and are suited to high-accuracy tasks, but they impose greater computational demands. The study therefore compares response quality, faithfulness, performance, and efficiency while highlighting the trade-off between model scale and computational resources.

Narrative, section by section

6 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract—Accurate and contextually faithful responses are

The study evaluates large language models on queries related to quranic studies. It examines their response accuracy, relevance, and faithfulness when supported by domain-specific information.

I.

Large language models can perform a wide range of activities, including summarization, translation, domain-specific question answering, and annotation. The unit examines their use in Quranic studies and compares 13 open-source models in terms of accuracy, faithfulness, performance, and efficiency. Their use in religious or culturally sensitive settings raises concerns about accuracy, contextual relevance, authenticity, distortion, and hallucination.

II.

Large language models generate responses to questions about Qur’anic studies from descriptions retrieved by the Retrieval-Augmented Generation system. The study evaluates their Context Relevance, Answer Faithfulness, and Answer Relevance in a zero-shot setting without fine-tuning on the dataset.

III.

The large language models are evaluated on context relevance, answer faithfulness, and answer relevance. They are grouped into large, medium, and small categories according to parameter size.

IV.

Large language models are evaluated across context relevance, answer faithfulness, and answer relevance in a Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework. Their performance varies with model size, and the largest models generally produce higher-quality responses but require more computational resources.

V.

Large language models were evaluated on Quranic studies-related queries within a Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework. Their performance varied by size, with larger models generally performing better but requiring more computational resources.

large models in Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models

Zahra Khalila, Arbi Haza Nasution, Winda Monika, Aytug Onan, Yohei Murakami, Yasir Bin Ismail Radi, Noor Mohammad Osmani · 2025

Large language models include Llama3:70b, Gemma2:27b, and QwQ:32b. They outperform medium and small models by capturing query semantics, producing accurate and contextually grounded responses, and showing stronger context understanding, faithfulness, and relevance. Their larger parameter sizes improve context relevance and reduce hallucination, and they benefit most from Retrieval-Augmented Generation. However, substantial memory and processing needs limit use in resource-constrained environments.

Large models, including Llama3:70b, Llama3.1:70b, Llama3.3:70b, Gemma2:27b, and QwQ:32b, generally outperform medium and small models across the three evaluation criteria. They show stronger context understanding, faithfulness, and relevance, but their substantial memory and processing requirements limit their use in resource-constrained environments.

Large Language Models in Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation

Shijie Wang, Wenqi Fan, Yue Feng, Shanru Lin, Xinyu Ma, Shuaiqiang Wang, Dawei Yin · 2025

Large Language Models are large models that acquire broad knowledge and exceptional language-understanding capabilities through training on extensive, wide-ranging data. They can support next-generation recommender systems by interpreting user profiles, item descriptions, and historical interactions. Their use is limited by hallucinations and insufficient up-to-date or domain-specific knowledge. In K-RagRec, a frozen model receives recommendation prompts and historical items, optionally with retrieved knowledge sub-graphs, and generates recommendations. Retrieved knowledge graphs help it use structural information without long context input.

Narrative, section by section

5 sections; each heading opens the text

Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation / Abstract

Large Language Models have achieved remarkable results and show potential for next-generation recommender systems. In LLM-based recommendation, they are limited by hallucinations and a lack of up-to-date and domain-specific knowledge.

1

Large Language Models acquire broad knowledge and language-understanding capabilities by training on extensive data. They enable recommender systems to interpret user profiles, item descriptions, and historical interactions.

2

Language models are combined with retrieval systems in RAG to guide text generation. In recommendations, knowledge sub-graphs from knowledge graphs are proposed to enhance language model performance.

3 / 3.1 .. 3.8

The large language model receives a recommendation prompt and user historical items, optionally augmented with retrieved knowledge sub-graphs, to generate a recommendation. Its parameters are frozen during K-RagRec training.

5

Large language models are supported by K-RagRec in making recommendations using retrieved knowledge from knowledge graphs. The framework helps them leverage structural information while avoiding long context input.

large language models in LightRAG: Simple and Fast Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Zirui Guo, Lianghao Xia, Yanhua Yu, Tu Ao, Chao Huang · 2025

Large language models are technology used to analyze text, identify entities and relationships, generate profiles, keywords, and answers, and produce meaningful outputs from queries and retrieved information. Their most important role in these records is within Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems, which supply external knowledge to improve usefulness, factual grounding, accuracy, contextual relevance, and domain-specific responses. The account begins with their enhancement through external retrieval, follows their indexing and generation tasks in LightRAG, and ends with efforts to improve their interpretation of graph-structured data.

Narrative, section by section

5 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Large language models are enhanced by Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems that integrate external knowledge sources. The unit describes LightRAG as a framework intended to improve the information supplied to these models.

Introduction

Large language models are enhanced by RAG systems that supply external knowledge. This integration is described as improving their usefulness in real-world applications and enabling more accurate and contextually relevant responses.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Large language models are leveraged by the generation component to produce meaningful outputs from the query and retrieved information.

The LightRAG Architecture / Graph-based Text Indexing .. Complexity Analysis of LightRAG

The large language model analyzes text chunks to identify entities and relationships, generates profiles and key-value pairs, extracts query keywords, and produces answers from retrieved information.

Related Work / Retrieval-Augmented Generation .. Large Language Model for Graphs

Large language models receive externally retrieved information in Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems to support more factually grounded and domain-specific responses. Researchers are also working to improve their ability to interpret graph-structured data.

Large Language Models in MAIN-RAG: Multi-Agent Filtering Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Chia-Yuan Chang, Zhimeng Jiang, Vineeth Rakesh, Menghai Pan, Chin-Chia Michael Yeh, Guanchu Wang, Mingzhi Hu, Zhichao Xu, Yan Zheng, Mahashweta Das, Na Zou · 2025

Large Language Models are NLP models and essential tools for various natural language processing tasks. They achieve state-of-the-art performance in question answering, summarization, and text generation, but reliance on static pre-trained data can produce outdated or incorrect information. During inference, irrelevant or noisy retrieved documents can mislead them: they are vulnerable to noise and often fail to reject irrelevant content. In MAIN-RAG, their agents collaboratively filter and score retrieved documents.

Narrative, section by section

3 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Large Language Models are becoming essential tools for various natural language processing tasks but often generate outdated or incorrect information. In MAIN-RAG, their agents collaboratively filter and score retrieved documents.

1 / Introduction

Large Language Models have achieved state-of-the-art performance across tasks including question answering, summarization, and text generation. Their reliance on static pre-trained data can lead to outdated or factually incorrect information.

2 / Preliminaries / 2.1 / Notations and Objectives .. 2.3 / Related Work

Large language models can be misled by irrelevant or noisy retrieved documents during inference. Existing studies cited in the unit find that they are vulnerable to noise and often fail to reject irrelevant content.

advanced language models in Mitigating the Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) via Pure Synthetic Data

Shenglai Zeng, Jiankun Zhang, Pengfei He, Jie Ren, Tianqi Zheng, Hanqing Lu, Han Xu, Hui Liu, Yue Xing, Jiliang Tang · 2025

Advanced language models receive queries and retrieved information, combining pre-trained knowledge with retrieval data to respond; the proposed approach uses synthetic rather than original retrieval data. They generate RAG outputs and synthetic data and support attribute identification, extraction, generation, privacy assessment, and rewriting; Stage-1 models may differ. Their benefits must be balanced with individual privacy rights.

Narrative, section by section

4 sections; each heading opens the text

Introduction

The large language model receives a query together with retrieved information and uses both its pre-trained knowledge and the retrieval data to generate a response. In the proposed approach, it is provided with synthetic retrieval data rather than original data.

Related Works

Large language models are used in RAG systems to generate outputs from retrieved information. Researchers also use them to generate synthetic data through zero-shot prompting and other methods for tasks including text classification and question answering.

Methods

LLMs are used for attribute identification, information extraction, data generation, privacy assessment, and rewriting. The models used for the Stage-1 components may be the same or different.

Ethic Statement

Advanced language models are presented as providing benefits that must be balanced with the protection of individual privacy rights.

large language models in Rationale-Guided Retrieval Augmented Generation

Jiwoong Sohn · 2025

Large language models are a model class and language models with significant potential in biomedicine, where they perform across tasks including USMLE-style question answering. Their adoption in high-stakes areas is limited by hallucinations, outdated knowledge, and vulnerability to irrelevant or unhelpful context. They generate output tokens conditioned on a query and retrieved documents, can use intrinsic parametric knowledge or external retrieved information, and may generate rationales and answers. Reviewed uses can increase computational costs, API costs, and inference latency; RAG2 improves performance by up to 6.1%.

Narrative, section by section

4 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Large language models have significant potential for applications in biomedicine but struggle with hallucinations and outdated knowledge. RAG2 improves the performance of state-of-the-art large language models of varying sizes by up to 6.1%.

Introduction

Large language models have demonstrated strong performance across biomedical tasks, including USMLE-style question answering. Their adoption in high-stakes areas is limited by hallucination and the difficulty of updating their knowledge.

2 / 2.1 .. 2.2

Large language models are used in several reviewed methods for adaptive RAG, rationale generation, verification, or fine-tuning. These uses can increase computational costs, API costs, and inference latency.

3 / 3.1 .. 3.4

The LLM generates output tokens conditioned on the query and retrieved documents. It is evaluated both with intrinsic parametric knowledge and with external retrieved information, and the same LLM is used to generate rationales and answer questions.

base large language model in Rationale-Guided Retrieval Augmented Generation

Jiwoong Sohn · 2025

The base large language model generates rationales whose perplexity differences train a filtering model and help filter question-document pairs. Its rationales can guide retrieval. Evaluated with and without retrieval, it is the system RAG2 aims to improve, with state-of-the-art LLMs showing better medical-question accuracy.

2 / 2.1 .. 2.2

The base large language model generates rationales whose perplexity differences provide detailed training signals for the filtering model.

5 / 5.1 .. 5.3

LLMs are evaluated with and without retrieval capabilities. The unit indicates that LLM rationales can guide retrieval and that rationale perplexity can be used to filter question-document pairs.

6

Large language models are the systems whose reliability, performance, and accuracy RAG2 is designed to improve. Various state-of-the-art LLMs showed improved accuracy with RAG2 across multiple medical question answering benchmarks.

large language models in Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability

Jeongyeon Hwang, Junyoung Park, Hyejin Park, Dongwoo Kim, Sangdon Park, Jungseul Ok · 2025

Large language models are models with limited internal knowledge. They perform strongly across tasks but can produce incorrect outputs when current knowledge is absent and misaligned or hallucinated responses when given irrelevant or misinformation documents. Retrieval-Augmented Generation supplements them with external databases, and filtering reduces such misaligned outputs.

Narrative, section by section

3 sections; each heading opens the text

front matter .. Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Estimation of Source Reliability / Abstract

Large language models have limited internal knowledge, which Retrieval-Augmented Generation supplements with information from external databases.

Introduction

Large language models demonstrate strong performance across various tasks but often produce incorrect outputs, especially when handling up-to-date knowledge absent from their internal knowledge.

C

LLMs often generate correct or hallucinated responses that are not grounded in irrelevant retrieved documents, with a similar pattern for misinformation documents. Filtering reduces these misaligned outputs.

Claims

large language models in SEAKR: Self-aware Knowledge Retrieval for Adaptive Retrieval Augmented Generation

Zijun Yao · 2025

Large language models are probabilistic distributions conditioned on input context that produce continuations, with parametric knowledge and internal states. They can answer from that knowledge, but may generate factual errors that appear correct when questions exceed its boundaries; their uncertainty concerns generated content and can be reflected in internal states. In retrieval augmented generation and reasoning, they generate answers, rationales, token probabilities, retrieval decisions, hidden EOS representations, and uncertainty evaluations. SEAKR uses these signals to extract self-aware uncertainty, choose whether and how to retrieve knowledge and reasoning strategies, and support final answers and complex tasks. This approach currently requires internal-state access; widely adopted models, including the GPT series, are commercially controlled, while retrieval integration may be misused to automate cyber manhunt.

Narrative, section by section

7 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Large language models provide internal states from which Self-aware Knowledge Retrieval extracts self-aware uncertainty. They use retrieved knowledge and selected reasoning strategies to support generation and complex tasks.

Introduction

Large language models can produce factually incorrect answers that appear correct, especially when queries exceed their limited parametric knowledge boundaries. They can also extract correct answers from their own parametric knowledge and exhibit self-aware uncertainty in their internal states.

2 / 2.1 .. 2.2

A Large Language Model generates answers in retrieval augmented generation and can be used for reasoning in retrieval augmented reasoning. Its output tokens, retrieval decisions, and internal hidden representations are discussed as possible sources for assessing whether retrieval is needed or whether generated content is factual.

3 .. 3.4

The large language model takes a context as input and outputs a continuation. SEAKR uses its generated rationales, token probabilities, hidden EOS representations, and uncertainty evaluations to decide when and how to retrieve knowledge and to produce the final answer.

6

SEAKR extracts self-aware uncertainty from LLMs’ internal states.

Limitations

SEAKR currently requires access to the internal states of large language models, although the authors aim to estimate self-aware uncertainty from model outputs instead. The most powerful and widely adopted large language models remain controlled by commercial companies, including the GPT series.

Ethical Considerations

Large language models are the systems whose factual correctness and trustworthiness retrieval augmented generation is intended to improve. SEAKR is developed upon open-sourced large language models, while integrating LLMs with information retrieval systems may be misused to automate cyber manhunt.

LLM in SafeRAG: Benchmarking Security in Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Xun Liang, Simin Niu, Zhiyu Li, Sensen Zhang, Hanyu Wang, Feiyu Xiong, Jason Zhaoxin Fan, Bo Tang, Jihao Zhao, Jiawei Yang, Shichao Song, Mengwei Wang · 2025

LLM is a language model that generates a final answer from a prompt containing an instruction, query, and filtered retrieved contexts. External knowledge supports knowledge-intensive tasks, but its incorporation increases vulnerability: attackers can tamper with texts, manipulate knowledge, induce refusals, alter key facts under counterfactual conflicts, or bypass even advanced models. Although it can detect toxicity, handle some conflicts, and prioritize evidence over injected DoS text, misleading contexts can still affect it.

Large language models use external knowledge in retrieval-augmented generation to support knowledge-intensive tasks. The text reports that attackers can manipulate knowledge to perform attack tasks against them, and that even advanced models can be bypassed.

Introduction

Large language models can use externally retrieved knowledge through retrieval-augmented generation. The text notes that advanced large language models show capabilities in detecting toxicity and handling some conflicts, but they remain vulnerable to tampered external texts and certain refusal-inducing attacks.

Large language models may incorrectly alter key facts when generating counterfactual conflict perturbations. They may also prioritize evidence over injected DoS attack text or be induced to refuse responses by misleading contexts.

large language models in SimGRAG: Leveraging Similar Subgraphs for Knowledge Graphs Driven Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Yuzheng Cai, Zhenyue Guo, Yiwen Pei, Wanrui Bian, Weiguo Zheng · 2025

Large language models are pre-trained models characterized as general, flexible, and increasingly versatile across diverse tasks. They can understand and handle knowledge graph construction, completion, and embedding, and can be integrated with Graph Neural Networks for graph data. Their main limitation is that hallucinations or outdated internal knowledge can yield unsatisfactory outputs. In SimGRAG, a large language model first interprets a user query and generates a small, query-aligned pattern graph, then uses retrieved and verbalized knowledge-graph subgraphs as evidence to generate a final answer. This evidence-supported use performs better than direct pre-trained-model use without evidence. Reported query-to-pattern alignment for Llama 3 70B reaches 98% on MetaQA and 93% on FactKG for queries of up to 3 hops. SimGRAG remains competitive across Llama 3 70B, Phi4-14B, and Qwen2.5-72B, but depends on effective instruction following; lower-quality models particularly weaken advanced-reasoning queries.

Narrative, section by section

7 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Large language models are described as increasingly versatile across various tasks. In SimGRAG, an LLM transforms queries into desired graph patterns.

Introduction

Large language models are described as general and flexible tools for diverse applications, but they can produce hallucinations or rely on outdated knowledge. In SimGRAG, a large language model generates a small pattern graph from the query and later uses the retrieved subgraphs to generate the final answer.

Related Work

Large language models have shown the ability to understand and handle knowledge graph-related tasks, including knowledge graph construction, completion, and embedding. They have also been integrated with Graph Neural Networks to enhance modeling capabilities for graph data, and they may produce unsatisfactory outputs because of hallucination or outdated internal knowledge.

Preliminaries

Large language models are used together with retrieved evidence from a knowledge graph to generate answers in Knowledge Graph Driven Retrieval-Augmented Generation.

The SimGRAG Approach / Query-to-Pattern Alignment .. Verbalized Subgraph-Augmented

The large language model generates query-aligned pattern graphs and later produces answers from verbalized retrieved subgraphs. Llama 3 70B achieved reported query-to-pattern alignment accuracies of 98% on MetaQA and 93% on FactKG for queries involving up to 3 hops.

Experiments .. Overall Latency

Large language models are evaluated both directly and within SimGRAG. SimGRAG remains competitive across Llama 3 70B, Phi4-14B, and Qwen2.5-72B, while direct use of pre-trained models without evidence produces comparatively poor performance.

Limitations

The large language model must understand and follow instructions effectively during query-to-pattern alignment and verbalized subgraph-augmented generation. Lower-quality or less capable models can reduce SimGRAG's performance, particularly on queries requiring advanced reasoning.

Large Language Models in SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains

Ran Xu, Hui Liu, Sreyashi Nag, Zhenwei Dai, Yaochen Xie, Xianfeng Tang, Chen Luo, Yang Li, Joyce C. Ho, Carl Yang, Qi He · 2025

Large Language Models are models with question-answering abilities that use external knowledge through retrieval-augmented generation. They can struggle with distribution shifts and accurately extracting information in specialized, domain-specific contexts. In SimRAG, a single Large Language Model is fine-tuned on instruction-following, question-answering, search-related, and general retrieval-oriented tasks; it then generates domain-relevant questions, candidate questions and answers, and answers from queries and retrieved contexts. Stage-II adapts it to specialized domains through synthetic data, supporting self-improvement and reducing data-generation costs.

SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains

Large Language Models are the models that SimRAG is intended to adapt to specialized domains.

Abstract

Large language models use external knowledge through retrieval-augmented generation to improve question answering. In SimRAG, the model is fine-tuned on instruction-following, question-answering, and search-related data, then prompted to generate domain-relevant questions.

Introduction

Large language models can struggle with distribution shifts and extracting information from domain-specific contexts. SimRAG fine-tunes a single large language model for both question answering with context and question generation from context.

Related Work

A large language model can serve as the generator in a retrieval-augmented generation system and can be fine-tuned for retrieval and question answering. In SimRAG, the same LLM generates candidate questions and answers, enabling self-improvement and reducing data-generation costs.

Methodology / Problem Setup .. Stage-II: Domain Adaptive Fine-tuning

The LLM generates answers from queries and retrieved contexts. It is fine-tuned in Stage-I on general retrieval-oriented tasks and then adapted in Stage-II to specialized domains through synthetic data.

large language model in TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text

Songshuo Lu · 2025

The large language model is a large language model used to process retrieved context and generate outputs, serving as the generator in Retrieval–Augmented Generation. It computes queries, keys, values, attention scores, hidden states, and KV caches during prefill and autoregressive decoding; its per-token cost spans layers and is characterized by L, H, K, dh, d, and dmlp. It employs Swiglu and can adapt to varied positional embeddings. In TurboRAG, it is coupled with a dense retriever and lightly supervised fine-tuned to consume a new cache layout, attention mask matrix, position embeddings, and concatenated document KV caches without question-answering accuracy regression. Its flexibility supports this approach, but TurboRAG’s fine-tuning dependency prevents direct application to newly emerging state-of-the-art large language models.

Narrative, section by section

6 sections; each heading opens the text

1 / Introduction .. Contributions

The large language model is coupled with a dense retriever in Retrieval–Augmented Generation. TurboRAG applies lightweight supervised fine-tuning so the model can consume the new cache layout.

2 / Related Work

A large language model serves as the generator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation, where it uses externally retrieved knowledge to support generation.

3 / Methodology .. 3.4 / The TurboRAG Pipeline

The large language model computes queries, keys, values, attention scores, and hidden states during prefill and decoding. In TurboRAG, it is fine-tuned with the new attention mask matrix and position embeddings so it can use concatenated document KV caches without question-answering accuracy regression.

5 / Conclusion and Discussion .. Limitations

The unit reports that large language models show flexibility with varied positional embeddings, drawing a parallel to context-extension techniques. It also notes that TurboRAG currently cannot be directly applied to newly emerging state-of-the-art large language models without addressing its fine-tuning dependency.

references

The unit cites work on large language models involving long-context understanding, retrieval, efficient attention, speculative decoding, and inference serving. It includes references to BERT, Llama 3, Qwen2, in-context retrieval-augmented language models, and methods for extending or efficiently processing model context.

G / Computational Load Calculation

The large language model is characterized by the parameters L, H, K, dh, d, and dmlp. Its computational cost is calculated per token across its layers.

Manan Suri, Puneet Mathur, Franck Dernoncourt, Kanika Gowswami, Ryan A. Rossi, and Dinesh Manocha · 2025

Large language models are technology that has advanced substantially but struggles to integrate external knowledge and adapt to unseen data. Retrieval Augmented Generation addresses these gaps by prompting them with retrieved textual or visual context to curate evidence, build reasoning chains, assess cross-modal consistency, and answer questions. They support multi-image, long-context QA, but safety limitations, hallucination, reliability, and accuracy remain concerns.

Narrative, section by section

4 sections; each heading opens the text

Related Work

Large Language Models have achieved significant advancements but still encounter challenges integrating external knowledge and adapting to new, unseen data. Retrieval Augmented Generation is described as addressing these gaps.

VisDoMRAG / 5.1 .. 5.2

The large language model is prompted with retrieved textual or visual context to curate evidence, construct reasoning chains, and generate answers. In Modality Fusion, it evaluates consistency between the reasoning chains from the two modalities.

Experiments / 6.1 .. 6.2

LLMs are used for end-to-end QA with multi-image and long-context capabilities. The evaluated models are Gemini-1.5-Flash, ChatGPT-4o, and Qwen2-VL-7B-Instruct.

Limitations

Large language models are associated with inherent AI safety limitations and the risk of hallucination. Their use in the approach contributes to concerns about the reliability and accuracy of generated outputs.

Large Language Models in SafetyRAG: Towards Safe Large Language Model-Based Application through Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Sihem Omri, Manel Abdelkader, and Mohamed Hamdi · 2025-02-17

Large Language Models are powerful Artificial Intelligence tools and deep learning models that handle question-answering, text-generation, and translation, including business applications. Despite fine-tuning and reinforcement learning for alignment with human values, they can be induced to produce offensive content through unsafe prompts, jailbreaks, prompt injection, or malicious fine-tuning. Safety facts retrieved as added context can reinforce learned values, describe unsafe consequences, and help models refuse unsafe requests. SafetyRAG supports this incorporation of appropriate safety facts, but its effectiveness depends on the underlying alignment of the base model.

Narrative, section by section

4 sections; each heading opens the text

I. INTRODUCTION

Large Language Models are described as powerful AI tools trained for tasks including question-answering, text generation, and translation. They are used in business applications and can be vulnerable to adversarial prompt injection attacks despite fine-tuning and reinforcement learning intended to align them with human values.

II. LITERATURE REVIEW / A. Threats of Unsafe Prompts for LLMs .. B. Unsafe Prompt Mitigation

LLMs can be induced to produce offensive content despite safety alignment. They are also vulnerable to unsafe prompts, jailbreak attacks, prompt injection, and malicious fine-tuning.

III. MATERIALS AND METHODS / A. Overall Framework .. 2) Baseline LLM models

The large language model is supported by retrieved safety facts that describe unsafe situations and their potential consequences. The added context is intended to reinforce learned values and help the model refuse unsafe requests.

V. CONCLUSION

Large language models are helped by SafetyRAG to incorporate appropriate safety facts into their responses. The underlying alignment of the base model affects how effective SafetyRAG is.

large language models in Ragas: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation

Shahul Es, Jithin James, Luis Espinosa-Anke, Steven Schockaert · 2025-04-28

Large language models capture enough knowledge to rival human performance on many question-answering benchmarks, but cannot answer questions about post-training events and struggle with rarely mentioned knowledge. They can receive knowledge from textual databases through RAG systems, acting as a natural-language layer and reducing hallucination risk. They are used to estimate factuality and evaluate generated text through prompting, token probabilities, hidden-state classifiers, and answer sampling. They can also verify whether statements follow from context, generate questions from answers, and extract relevant context sentences.

Narrative, section by section

4 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Large language models receive knowledge from a reference textual database through RAG systems. This enables them to act as a natural language layer between users and textual databases and helps reduce the risk of hallucinations.

Introduction

Large Language Models capture enough knowledge to rival human performance across a wide range of question answering benchmarks. Even the largest models share limitations involving post-training events and rarely mentioned knowledge.

2 .. Faithfulness

Large language models are used to estimate factuality and evaluate generated text through prompting, token probabilities, hidden-state classifiers, and answer sampling. In the described implementation and experiments, prompts are evaluated with gpt-3.5-turbo-16k through the OpenAI API.

opening .. The WikiEval Dataset

The large language model determines whether statements can be inferred from a context using a verification function. It also generates potential questions from an answer and extracts context sentences relevant to a question.

large language models in Knowledge Graph-Guided Retrieval Augmented Generation

Xiangrong Zhu · 2025-04-29/2025-05-04

Large language models are models that generate responses. They have achieved success in real-world question answering, writing assistance, and code generation, but their responses may contain hallucinations. Retrieval-augmented generation seeks to address this by supplying retrieved or organized chunks with the user query, incorporating documents or structured knowledge into prompts, extracting entities and relations, and generating response context. They are a representative achievement of contemporary artificial intelligence and may address knowledge graph completion and knowledge graph question answering.

Narrative, section by section

4 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Large language models generate responses that may contain hallucinations, which retrieval-augmented generation seeks to address.

1

Large language models have achieved success in tasks including question answering, writing assistance, and code generation. Their responses can be improved with retrieved documents or structured knowledge incorporated into prompts.

2 / 2.1 .. 2.3

LLMs receive retrieved or organized chunks together with the user query for response generation. The unit presents LLM prompts as a way to extract entities and relations from chunks and to generate the final response context.

4

Large language models are described as a representative achievement of contemporary artificial intelligence and as having the potential to address knowledge graph completion and knowledge graph question answering. In retrieval-augmented generation systems, their generation can be assisted by retrieved document chunks.

LLMs in RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models

Bang An · 2025-04-29/2025-05-04

LLMs are technologies that support many tasks by generating responses from user queries and, in RAG settings, retrieved documents; non-RAG pipelines rely on knowledge stored in the model. Although they are aligned with human values through several development approaches and evaluated for safety, they remain susceptible to unsafe content. A comparative analysis of eleven LLMs examines safety in RAG and non-RAG frameworks, finding that safety can change with RAG and that most LLMs in the RAG setting show a higher percentage of unsafe responses. The study seeks to uncover overlooked RAG vulnerabilities.

Narrative, section by section

6 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

The study conducts a comparative analysis of RAG and non-RAG frameworks using eleven LLMs. It finds that their safety can change when they are used with RAG.

Introduction

Large language models can support many tasks but are susceptible to creating unsafe content. The unit examines their safety in non-RAG and RAG settings.

Related Work

LLMs are aligned with human values through supervised learning, RLHF, safety-specific examples, system-level guardrails, controllable safe generation, interpretability, unlearning, and safety evaluation. Red-teaming is used to identify their vulnerabilities.

Definitions

The LLM G takes an instruction, retrieved documents, and a user query as input to generate a response. In a standard non-RAG pipeline, it instead relies on knowledge stored in the model.

Limitations

The general LLMs are the focus of the study's analysis of safety behaviors in retrieval-augmented generation settings.

Ethics Statement

The paper aims to uncover vulnerabilities of LLMs in the RAG setting that people have overlooked.

large language models in Enhancing treatment decision-making for low back pain: a novel framework integrating large language models with retrieval-augmented generation technology

Rong Chen, Siyun Zhang, Yiyi Zheng, Qiuhua Yu and Chuhuai Wang · 2025-05-14

Large language models are transformer-based language-processing models that use large-scale text data to simulate language understanding and generation. In the proposed clinical decision-support framework for chronic low back pain, they process patient complaints, interact with retrieved medical knowledge, analyze unstructured medical data, synthesize complex clinical variables, and generate recommendations. Their central value is support for clinical decision-making, current information, content creation, and interaction. Their central limitation is possible hallucinations, inaccurate fact generation, erroneous responses, and reliance on public-domain data. The framework integrates them with retrieval-augmented generation and evaluates performance against GPT-4.0, ERNIE Bot, and DeepSeek; the hybrid approach provides more explicit grounding in clinical workflow constraints than pure LLM approaches.

4 sections; each heading opens the text

front matter .. Enhancing treatment decision-making for low back pain: a novel framework integrating large language models with retrieva

Large language models were integrated into a clinical decision-support framework for chronic low back pain. Their performance was evaluated through comparison with GPT-4.0, ERNIE Bot, and DeepSeek.

1 Introduction

Large language models use transformer architectures and large-scale text data to simulate human language understanding and generation. They can analyze unstructured medical data and support clinical decision-making, but their use in clinical practice is limited by the possibility of hallucinations and erroneous responses.

2 Materials and methods / 2.1 Framework .. 2.4 LtM prompting

Large language models are used to process patient complaints, interact with retrieved medical knowledge, and generate decision recommendations. The unit notes that they can provide current information and support content creation and interaction, but may generate inaccurate facts and depend on public-domain training data.

5 Discussion

Large language models are used for semantic analysis, synthesis of complex clinical variables, and generation of clinical recommendations. The unit contrasts the hybrid approach with pure LLM approaches, which are described as having greater hallucination risk and less explicit grounding in clinical workflow constraints.

Large Language Models (LLMs) in Retrieval augmented generation for large language models in healthcare: A systematic review

Lameck Mbangula Amugongo · 2025-06-11

Large Language Models (LLMs) are AI systems and a natural language processing technology that generate coherent, contextually relevant content. They have promising capabilities for complex tasks and can revolutionise natural language processing across domains, including healthcare. In healthcare, they can support retrieval, query augmentation, document summarization, response generation, feature extraction, and medical reasoning. Their use is constrained by training data that may be months old, inaccurate, nonsensical, biased, harmful, or unsafe outputs, hallucinations, limited transparency and explainability, contextual-data difficulties, memorized training data, and possible data leakage. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is intended to ground LLMs with up-to-date, user-specific information and external medical knowledge: the model generates a response from a user query and retrieved context. RAG can improve accuracy, factuality, consistency, and safety, and LLM-based RAG systems can outperform standalone models and some other approaches in medical tasks. Yet RAG does not prevent incorrect answers or explanations. LLMs are evaluated for correctness, relevance, faithfulness, fluency, and related qualities, while ethical and regulatory considerations remain necessary for healthcare acceptance and adoption.

Narrative, section by section

8 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Large Language Models (LLMs) are described as having promising capabilities for complex tasks in critical sectors such as healthcare. Their limitations include outdated training data, hallucinated or inaccurate content, and a lack of transparency in generated content.

Introduction

Large Language Models have demonstrated strong capabilities in generating coherent and contextually relevant text across natural language processing tasks, including healthcare applications. Their use in healthcare is limited by inaccurate or nonsensical outputs, bias, harmful answers, and difficulties with contextual data.

Methods .. Exclusion criteria

LLMs are the systems that RAG is intended to ground with up-to-date and user-specific information. The review examines their use with RAG in healthcare and extracts information about the LLMs used in the selected studies.

Results / Included studies .. Datasets

Large language models are augmented with external medical knowledge sources to generate clinically correct responses. The review describes RAG methods intended to reduce outdated information and fabricated responses.

RAG overview .. Advanced RAG

A large language model generates responses using the user’s query together with retrieved context. The unit describes LLMs as being limited by the age of their training data, while RAG can improve their accuracy, factuality, consistency, and safety in healthcare tasks.

Modular RAG

A large language model is used in the described systems for retrieval, query augmentation, document summarization, response generation, feature extraction, and medical reasoning. The unit reports that LLM-based RAG systems can outperform standalone models, traditional retrieval approaches, and some supervised methods in medical tasks.

Evaluation metrics and frameworks

Large language models are evaluated in RAG applications using metrics for correctness, relevance, faithfulness, fluency, and other output qualities. One study compared general and biomedical LLMs across medical question-answering tasks using multiple corpora and retrievers.

Ethical considerations

Large language models may generate incorrect answers and explanations even when RAG is used. Their high output variability, limited inherent explainability, memorized training data, and potential for hallucination, bias, data leakage, and unsafe outputs create ethical and regulatory challenges in healthcare.

Generative Pre-trained Transformers in Retrieval augmented generation for large language models in healthcare: A systematic review

Lameck Mbangula Amugongo · 2025-06-11

Generative Pre-trained Transformers are large language models that generate coherent, contextually relevant text and serve as generative backbones for retrieval augmented generation in healthcare. Reviewed studies predominantly use proprietary models, while open-source models generally have lower performance and more limited context windows. Their healthcare use may shape care and enhance patient care through continuous improvement, but most studies lack safety considerations. Progress requires stronger evidence integration, longer-context handling, diverse benchmarks, healthcare-specific evaluation, multimodal data, and ethical adoption.

Narrative, section by section

4 sections; each heading opens the text

Data analysis

Large language models are used as the generative backbones of RAG systems in healthcare. The unit compares proprietary and open-source models and notes that open-source models generally have lower performance and more limited context windows.

Discussion

Large language models in healthcare are examined in relation to RAG applications, evaluation, multimodal data, and ethical adoption. The unit reports that proprietary models are used in 53 of the 70 reviewed studies and that future systems need stronger evidence integration, longer-context handling, diverse benchmarks, and healthcare-specific evaluation.

Conclusion

Large language models are grounded and improved for healthcare tasks through RAG. The text reports that proprietary LLMs are the models most commonly used in existing studies.

Author contributions

Large language models appear in the title as the technology considered in relation to retrieval augmented generation and healthcare.

Through GRAG, a frozen LLM receives query-relevant textual subgraphs, enhancing generation and potentially outperforming fine-tuned LLMs at reduced training cost.

Large Language Models in GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Yuntong Hu, Zhihan Lei, Zheng Zhang, Bo Pan, Chen Ling, Liang Zhao · 2025-07-12

Large Language Models are language models trained on large text corpora to develop language understanding. They provide text embeddings for textual node and edge attributes and contextual reasoning that supports graph reasoning and zero-shot graph answering. They demonstrate reasoning capabilities on graph-based data, yet textual training does not inherently provide understanding of complex graph-structured data, and they can make factual errors because of training-data limits and no real-time knowledge. Through GRAG, complementary text and graph views supply textual and graph information, helping them comprehend and use graph context more effectively for responses involving networked documents.

Narrative, section by section

3 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Large Language Models receive textual graphs through complementary text and graph views. These views enable them to more effectively comprehend and use graph context.

Introduction

Large Language Models demonstrate capabilities on reasoning tasks, including graph-based data, but struggle with factual errors because of limitations in training data and lack of real-time knowledge. In this unit, they are supplied with textual and graph information through GRAG to improve responses involving networked documents.

Related Work / Prompt Tuning .. Retrieval on Graphs

Large language models provide text embedding capabilities for encoding textual node and edge attributes and contextual reasoning capabilities for graph reasoning and zero-shot graph answering. Their training on large text corpora does not inherently equip them to understand or reason about complex graph-structured data.

LLM in Question Decomposition for Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Paul J. L. Ammann · 2025-07-28/2025-07-29

LLM is a large language model used in a pipeline grounded in verifiable external sources to produce more reliable answers. It decomposes original, complex queries into simpler fact-seeking subqueries without task-specific training. In the zero-shot setup, it generates at most five subqueries and usually exactly five, indicating a fixed prompt-defined budget rather than adaptation to question complexity. Although increasing capability supports this use, it has inherent limits with current or specialized knowledge, may lag specialized models in recall, and its choice affects subquery quality and adaptation across domains or languages.

Narrative, section by section

5 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Large language models are grounded in verifiable external sources to generate more reliable answers. In the proposed pipeline, an LLM decomposes an original query into sub-questions.

Introduction

Large language models are used by the question decomposition component to generate simpler, fact-seeking subqueries without task-specific training. The text also describes their increasing capability as enabling this approach.

opening .. Efficiency

The LLM generates at most five subqueries per query under the zero-shot experimental setup. It almost always generates exactly five, suggesting that it applies a fixed subquery budget rather than adapting the number of subqueries to question complexity.

Related Work / RAG augments LLMs with access to

Large language models have inherent limitations in handling up-to-date or specialized knowledge. They are also used to decompose complex questions and as synthetic data generators, although they may fail to match the recall performance of specialized models.

Limitations

The underlying large language model affects subquery quality, making model selection potentially necessary for adaptation to new domains or languages.

large language model in A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models

Qinggang Zhang, Shengyuan Chen, Yuanchen Bei, Zheng Yuan, Huachi Zhou, Zijin Hong, Hao Chen, Yilin Xiao, Chuang Zhou, Junnan Dong, Yi Chang, Xiao Huang · 2025-09-29

Large language models demonstrate remarkable natural language processing capabilities across a wide range of tasks, including text comprehension, question answering, and content generation. They perform strongly on general tasks, but specialized applications remain challenging: their broad pre-trained knowledge can be shallow in specialized fields, and they may have limited domain-specific accuracy, logical consistency, and handling of context-dependent interpretations. Knowledge limitations, reasoning complexity, context sensitivity, fixed context windows, and difficulty capturing long-range dependencies can reduce effectiveness, particularly when information is excessive or widely distributed. In GraphRAG, a large language model is the system that receives retrieved knowledge and combines it with inherent knowledge for reasoning and response generation. It functions as an intelligent agent for graph-based organization and integration: generating summaries, extracting facts, constructing knowledge graphs, supporting retrieval and planning, producing contextual embeddings and query expansions, interpreting graph content, identifying retrieval paths, and synthesizing multiple sources. It may be prompted with retrieved information to build more credible reasoning chains, assess content, decide when retrieval is needed, and generate labels or memory. GraphRAG enhances the model with structured context, runtime prompt augmentation, graph-based retrieval, and domain-specific background knowledge, improving complex-query performance. The model can be adapted through fine-tuning, in-context learning, or combination with graph and domain-specific models. However, it is not inherently equipped for graph-structured data, and large graph problems remain difficult because of input-length limits. Future improvement focuses on aligning external structured knowledge with learned representations through knowledge distillation, fine-tuning, cross-modal integration, uncertainty modeling, and probabilistic reasoning.

Narrative, section by section

12 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract—Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated

Large language models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across a wide range of tasks. Their application to specialized domains remains challenging because it requires deep expertise.

I. INTRODUCTION

Large language models achieve strong results across general tasks but have limited ability in specialized domains because of knowledge limitations, reasoning complexity, and context sensitivity. They may struggle with domain-specific accuracy, logical consistency, and context-dependent interpretations.

II. OVERVIEW

Large language models are the systems into which GraphRAG integrates retrieved knowledge to support complex reasoning and generation.

III. WHAT IS GRAPHRAG / A. Traditional RAG Pipeline .. D. Traditional RAG vs GraphRAG

A large language model uses retrieved knowledge and its inherent knowledge to generate responses in RAG systems. Its fixed context window and difficulty capturing long-range dependencies can limit its ability to use excessive or widely distributed retrieved information.

IV. KNOWLEDGE ORGANIZATION .. C. Hybrid GraphRAG

The large language model functions as an intelligent agent that uses graph structures to organize and integrate information. It can also generate summaries, extract facts, construct knowledge graphs, and support retrieval or planning.

V. KNOWLEDGE RETRIEVAL / A. Overall Pipeline of Knowledge Retriever .. C. Retrieval Enhancement Strategies

A large language model contributes contextual embeddings and generative capabilities to retrieval. It can generate query expansions, interpret graph content, identify retrieval paths, and synthesize information from multiple sources.

VI. KNOWLEDGE INTEGRATION .. C. Integration Enhancement Strategies.

A large language model provides the foundational framework for knowledge integration, so the methods generally avoid modifying individual layers or completely reinitializing the model. It can be adapted through fine-tuning, prompted through in-context learning, or combined with graph and domain-specific models.

VII. CONCLUSION

LLMs demonstrate strong natural language processing capabilities across many tasks, but their effectiveness decreases in specialized, knowledge-intensive domains that are rarely represented in the pre-training corpus. They benefit from GraphRAG's well-organized background knowledge.

A. Open-Source Projects and Applications

Large language models are enhanced in the described systems through integration with knowledge graphs and graph-based retrieval. The unit states that GraphRAG can improve their performance on complex queries by providing runtime prompt augmentation, structured context, and domain-specific knowledge.

B. Limitations and Future Opportunities

The large language model must be aligned with external knowledge so that structured information is harmonized with its learned representations. Knowledge distillation, fine-tuning, cross-modal integration, uncertainty modeling, and probabilistic reasoning are identified as approaches for improving this alignment.

C. Discussion on GraphRAG

Large language models are used by city planners in the GraphRAG planning analogy to divide source documents, identify element instances, create summaries, and produce community reports. They are not inherently equipped to process graph-structured data, and their input-length limits make large graph problems difficult to handle.

D. Traditional RAG Pipeline

A large language model is prompted with retrieved information to construct more credible reasoning chains and generate informed content. It can also assess retrieved and generated content, decide when retrieval is necessary, and generate labels or memory used by RAG methods.

LLM in MEGA-RAG: a retrieval-augmented generation framework with multi-evidence guided answer refinement for mitigating hallucinations of LLMs in public health

Shan Xu, Zhaokun Yan, Chengxiao Dai and Fan Wu · 2025-10-08

Large language models are increasingly adopted in public health, but their hallucinations can mislead clinical communication, guidance, and policy decisions. Existing domain-specific fine-tuning, adversarial training, and retrieval-augmented generation with structured knowledge bases provide only partial mitigation. MEGA-RAG is designed to reduce these hallucinations through evidence-grounded generation: a large language model produces candidate answers from prompts containing a user question and retrieved evidence, rather than relying only on internal knowledge, with multi-evidence guided refinement and final answer fusion. In public-health scenarios, models are evaluated for hallucination reduction, answer reliability, and evidence-based responses using Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1 Score. Results compare standard and domain-specific models and show that unsupported or fabricated claims remain a concern without sufficient factual grounding.

LLMs in OG-RAG: Ontology-grounded retrieval-augmented generation for large language models

Kartik Sharma · 2025-11-04/2025-11-09

LLMs are language models widely used for generic tasks including question answering and search, and they have advanced question-answering systems, search engines, and generic chatbots. Their central limitation is adapting reliably to specialized, precise, knowledge-driven domains: they can require expensive fine-tuning or suboptimal retrieval, struggle with diverse domain structures and procedural-rule deduction, hallucinate during deductive reasoning, and provide responses that are hard to trace to context. Structured knowledge graphs, domain-specific grounding, fact-based reasoning, and retrieved ontology-grounded context are used to support them. In OG-RAG, they fill domain-specific ontology values, generate questions, answers, ratings, and context-based responses, and are evaluated across models and retrieval methods to improve controlled-vocabulary, structured-evidence use across domains.

Narrative, section by section

6 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Large language models are widely used for generic tasks such as question answering and search, but they struggle to adapt to specialized knowledge and knowledge-driven tasks without expensive fine-tuning or suboptimal retrieval methods. OG-RAG is evaluated across four large language models.

Introduction

Large language models have advanced question-answering systems, search engines, and generic chatbots, but they struggle with precise, domain-specific data and diverse domain structures. They also have difficulty reliably deducing conclusions from procedural rules and enabling users to trace responses to relevant context.

Related Work

LLMs benefit from structured knowledge graphs, domain-specific grounding, and fact-based reasoning. They are also described as flexible neural models that can hallucinate during deductive reasoning.

OG-RAG .. Relevant Hyeredges as Context

The large language model is used with a mapping prompt to fill domain-specific values into the ontology from document chunks. OG-RAG supplies it with retrieved, ontology-grounded context to support accurate domain-specific responses.

Experiments / Query answering .. Ontology sensitivity

Large language models are used to generate questions, answers, and ratings, and to produce responses from retrieved contexts. The experiments compare how different underlying models respond to contexts supplied by several retrieval methods.

Conclusion

Large language models are the systems that OG-RAG is intended to help adapt across domains. The method supports their use of controlled vocabulary and structured evidence retrieval.
